Which estimator, when, and how?

AMCEaverage marginal component effect OLSordinary least squares GLSgeneralized least squares Logitlogistic regression PPMLPoisson pseudo-maximum likelihood

Yifan Qi
Statistics Study Group
16 October 2026

∑i=1Nxi wi (yi−μi)=0\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i\, \nv{w_i}\,\bigl(y_i-\hl{\mu_i}\bigr)=0i=1∑N​xi​wi​(yi​−μi​)=0

All five solve this one equation. Choosing one means choosing the shape of μ\muμ, the weights www, and what you must assume for it to hold at the truth.

Today is about five tools most of us use or will meet: the AMCE (average marginal component effect) from conjoint experiments, OLS (ordinary least squares), GLS (generalized least squares), logit, and PPML (Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood). As PhD students we treat them as tools, so the questions are practical: which one, when, and how.

My answer rests on one idea: all five solve the equation on the right. They differ in three dials, the shape of the mean, the weights, and what you must assume for the equation to hold at the truth. Your outcome, your errors and your design set those dials, not taste. Two years ago I gave you eight assumptions for OLS; today they tell us what each tool costs.

直觉：五个估计方法是五件工具。挑哪件、什么时候用、怎么用，取决于结果变量长什么样、误差怎么相关、数据是怎么来的；它们底下解的是同一个方程。

The route: one example, five estimators, one equation

Here is the route, read from left to right; every box is one tool or the ground it stands on. On the left, where the number comes from: the eight assumptions you know, sorted into three questions, and a made-up job-offer experiment where we know the right answer, so the design hands us the AMCE. In the middle, the first estimator: the AMCE is a difference in means, which is OLS on a dummy, and OLS is the first appearance of the equation. Then four moves away from OLS: keep the estimate but fix the uncertainty when one person gives six answers; change the weights, which is GLS; change the shape of the mean to a logistic curve, which is logit; or to an exponential, which is PPML. On the right, what all five share: one estimating equation and one sandwich formula for the standard error.

Each box is a link. Every tool gets the same slide: its full name and when to use it, what it solves, what it assumes, when it breaks, and how to use it in practice. The full derivations sit in the appendix after the references, behind the Derivation button at the top right of each slide; I will open them only if you ask. Under each box: where its derivation slides are.

直觉：这张图回答“为什么按这个顺序讲”：左边定义我们要的数，中间从 OLS 出发，每次只改一样东西（不确定性、权重、均值形状），右边再合回同一个方程。

Each of the eight assumptions answers one of three questions

Two years ago: eight assumptions for OLS, A1 to A8, as one list. Today: the same eight, sorted by what they are for.

Estimandthe number we want, fixed before any data: how much a high salary raises the chance of accepting Estimatora rule that turns any data set into a number Estimatewhat the rule returns in the one sample we have

What number do I want?

estimand and identification

A1the mean is linear in the parameters
A4, A5the error averages zero at every xxx

If it fails: you get a different number, 0.55 instead of 0.33.

How do I compute it?

the estimator has one solution

A2no regressor copies the others (full rank)
A3salary takes both values

If it fails: there is no unique answer.

How sure am I?

inference: sampling and grouping

A3independent draws
A6every answer equally noisy
A7no two answers correlated
A8normal errors, for exact ttt tests

If it fails: the same number, with the wrong standard error.

When an assumption fails, first ask which question it was answering.

Two years ago, in the foundations session, I gave you eight assumptions for OLS (ordinary least squares) as one list. Today we keep all eight and sort them by the question each one answers. First, three words. The estimand is the number we want, fixed before we see any data: how much a high salary raises the chance that someone accepts a job offer. The estimator is a rule that turns any data set into a number. The estimate is what the rule returns in our one sample.

(Column 1.) What number do I want: that is identification. A1 says the mean is linear; A4 and A5 say the error averages zero at every value of x. If this fails you get a different number: 0.55 instead of 0.33, as the example will show. (Column 2.) How do I compute it: full rank, and salary must actually vary; otherwise there is no unique answer. (Column 3.) How sure am I: independent draws, equal variances, no correlation, and normality for exact t tests. If these fail, the number stays and only its standard error is wrong.

That is the habit for the rest of the talk: when an assumption fails, first ask which question it was answering. Every tool today is judged on these three questions. The full list, how the assumptions stack into levels, and the central limit theorem behind the large-sample tests are in the appendix, D1 to D6.

直觉：还是那八条，一条没变，只是按“要哪个数、怎么算出来、有多大把握”重新分组。哪条假设出了问题，先问它在回答哪个问题。

An estimator is a ruler: judge it by where its readings land

Estimand the length we want, fixed before anyone measures.

τS=E[Yi(1,Ri)−Yi(0,Ri)]=0.33\tau_S=E\bigl[Y_i(1,R_i)-Y_i(0,R_i)\bigr]=\hl{0.33}τS​=E[Yi​(1,Ri​)−Yi​(0,Ri​)]=0.33

Estimator the ruler: a rule written down before the data. Estimate one reading.

τ^=yˉ1−yˉ0=0.735−0.405=0.33\hat\tau=\bar y_1-\bar y_0=0.735-0.405=0.33τ^=yˉ​1​−yˉ​0​=0.735−0.405=0.33

Identification does the ruler touch only the table? Without a coin, remote work rides along with a high salary.

τ^=bS+δ bR=0.33+0.67×0.33=0.55\hat\tau=b_S+\delta\,b_R=0.33+0.67\times0.33=0.55τ^=bS​+δbR​=0.33+0.67×0.33=0.55

Repeat each fresh sample gives a new reading. Centred on the truth: unbiased. Their spread is what the SE (standard error) estimates.

E[τ^]=τS,Var⁡(τ^)=p1(1−p1)n1+p0(1−p0)n0=0.0272E[\hat\tau]=\tau_S,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\hat\tau)=\tfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}+\tfrac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n_0}=0.027^2E[τ^]=τS​,Var(τ^)=n1​p1​(1−p1​)​+n0​p0​(1−p0​)​=0.0272

More data four times the answers, half the spread. Without the coin the readings sharpen too, around 0.55.

sd⁡∝N−1/2\operatorname{sd}\propto N^{-1/2}sd∝N−1/2: 0.027 to 0.013; τ^→τS\hat\tau\to\tau_Sτ^→τS​ (consistency) only if identified

Before the tools, one picture to carry through the talk. The estimand is a length: how much a high salary raises the chance of accepting a job offer. It is fixed before anyone measures, and in real data nobody ever sees it. Here we can, the red line at 0.33, only because we built the example ourselves: offers with a high or low salary, remote or in the office.

(Step.) The estimator is a ruler: a rule written down before the data, here the acceptance rate under a high salary minus the rate under a low one. The estimate is one reading of that ruler on our one sample: 0.735 minus 0.405, which is 0.33.

(Step.) Identification asks whether the ruler touches only the table. Without a coin, high-salary offers are remote far more often, delta is two thirds, and remote work adds 0.33 of its own. The same ruler now reads 0.55: 0.33 plus two thirds of 0.33. The ruler is not broken; it measures the table and the cloth together. A coin that picks the salary pulls the cloth off; controlling for remote measures the cloth and subtracts it.

(Step.) Now imagine drawing a fresh sample and reading the ruler again, eighty times. The readings scatter. Their centre sits on the red line: that is unbiasedness, a property of the ruler, not of any one reading. Their spread, 0.027 for this difference in means, is what a standard error tries to estimate from the one sample we have. Adding remote as a control, as OLS will do, shrinks it to 0.0252. (Draw again redraws the eighty samples.)

(Step.) Four times the data halves the spread, because standard deviations fall with one over root N: the readings close in on the truth, which is consistency. But look at the grey cloud, the same ruler without the coin: it also gets sharper, around 0.55. More data makes a wrong reading more precise; only the design fixes it. That is why identification was the first of the three questions.

直觉：估计目标是桌子的真实长度，估计量是尺子（事先写好的计算规则），估计值是这一次的读数。识别问的是尺子量到的是不是只有桌子：没有随机化，远程办公像一块桌布搭在上面，读数变成 0.55。尺子好不好，要看反复抽样时读数落在哪里：中心对准真值就是无偏，散开的程度就是标准误要估计的东西。数据越多读数越集中，但识别错了，只会把错的数量得更精确。

A made-up example, so we know the right answer

200 people each see 6 job offers and say accept or not: N=1,200N=1{,}200N=1,200 answers.

Each offer has a salary SiS_iSi​ (1 high, 0 low) and remote work RiR_iRi​ (1 remote, 0 office). We wrote the acceptance rates ourselves:

E(yi∣Si,Ri)=0.24+0.33 Si+0.33 RiE(y_i\mid S_i,R_i)=0.24+0.33\,S_i+0.33\,R_iE(yi​∣Si​,Ri​)=0.24+0.33Si​+0.33Ri​

A high salary adds 0.33 to remote offers (0.90−0.57)(0.90-0.57)(0.90−0.57) and to office ones (0.57−0.24)(0.57-0.24)(0.57−0.24): one right answer, +0.33.

One person's six answers are correlated: some people say yes to almost anything.

Randomisedoffers shuffled: 300 answers per cell Observationalhigh salary comes with remote: 500 of 600 high-salary offers are remote, 100 of 600 low-salary ones

We need an example where we know the right answer, so I made one up. Two hundred people each look at six job offers, high or low salary, remote or office only, and say whether they would accept.

I fixed the four acceptance rates: 0.90, 0.57, 0.57 and 0.24. A high salary adds 0.33 whether the job is remote or not: one right answer, and we can grade every method against it.

(Widget.) Each dot is one answer, filled if accepted. Randomised: 300 answers per cell, and high minus low salary is 0.735 minus 0.405, exactly 0.330. Switch to observational: well-paid jobs tend to be remote, 500 of the 600 high-salary offers but only 100 of the 600 low-salary ones. The rates inside the cells have not changed, yet the same difference is 0.845 minus 0.295, 0.550. Only which offer went with which answer has changed.

One more fact for later: some people accept almost everything, so one person's six answers are correlated. Point at a dot to ring that person's answers. (The dots are the rows of job_offer_example.csv; both designs have exactly 684 acceptances.)

If you work with firm data, read this as a panel: 200 firms observed for six years instead of 200 people answering six offers. The observational design is what such data usually look like, the variable of interest travelling with other traits; the randomised design is what an experiment buys you.

直觉：例子是自己造的，标准答案事先就知道：高薪让接受率高 0.33。两种设计里四个格子的接受率一模一样，变的只是哪份 offer 落到了哪一行，可简单的均值差就从 0.33 变成了 0.55。

Salary travels with remote work, so the raw gap mixes two effects

Real offers attributes travel together: 500 of 600 high-salary offers are remote, only 100 of 600 low-salary ones.

q1=56q_1=\tfrac56q1​=65​ and q0=16q_0=\tfrac16q0​=61​: the share of remote offers at a high and at a low salary.

The raw gap salary's own effect, plus remote work riding along:

yˉ1−yˉ0=bS+δ bR,δ=q1−q0\bar y_1-\bar y_0=\nv{b_S}+\hl{\delta\,b_R},\qquad \delta=q_1-q_0yˉ​1​−yˉ​0​=bS​+δbR​,δ=q1​−q0​

0.55=0.33+0.67×0.330.55=0.33+\hl{0.67\times0.33}0.55=0.33+0.67×0.33, the omitted-variable identity of the OLS section.

Same mix give both salaries the same share of remote offers: δ=0\delta=0δ=0 and the rider is gone.

yˉ1−yˉ0=0.735−0.405=0.33\bar y_1-\bar y_0=0.735-0.405=0.33yˉ​1​−yˉ​0​=0.735−0.405=0.33. Same mix, change salary only: that is the AMCE (average marginal component effect).

Start from what real data look like. On page 5 the observational offers came bundled: 500 of 600 well-paid jobs were remote, but only 100 of 600 poorly paid ones. Call those shares q one and q zero. (Widget.) Each column is one salary. A bar's width is the share of those offers that are office or remote; its height is their acceptance rate. The dark line is the column's average, so the mix decides where it sits. High minus low: 0.845 minus 0.295, a gap of 0.55.

(Step.) Where does 0.55 come from? Salary itself adds b S, 0.33. But the high-salary column is also far more remote, and remote work adds b R, 0.33, wherever it appears. Delta, q one minus q zero, is two thirds. So two thirds of 0.33, about 0.22, rides along with salary: 0.55 is 0.33 plus 0.22. This is the omitted-variable identity we will meet again in the OLS section, drawn as a picture; it is exact here because our rates have no interaction.

(Step.) Now give both columns the same mix. Watch the red part shrink to nothing: the gap falls to 0.33. Same mix of everything else, change only the salary: that is what the AMCE, the average marginal component effect, asks for. Average, over evaluators; marginal, over the other attributes; component, one attribute. Drag the slider: any mix that differs between the two sides leaks remote work into the salary effect. Next page: what exactly the AMCE is.

直觉：现实里属性是一起变的，高薪的工作往往也是远程的。所以直接比较高薪和低薪，0.55 的差距里混着两样东西：薪水本身的 0.33，加上跟着薪水一起来的远程带来的 0.22。两边远程的比例一样，搭便车的那一截就消失了，差距正好是 0.33：这就是 AMCE 要的“组合一样，只换薪水”。

The AMCE: the average change between two possible answers

Two answers each offer has one answer at a high salary and one at a low salary, remote as drawn. We see only one of them.

Yi(1,Ri),  Yi(0,Ri);yi=Yi(Si,Ri)Y_i(1,R_i),\ \ Y_i(0,R_i);\qquad y_i=Y_i(S_i,R_i)Yi​(1,Ri​),  Yi​(0,Ri​);yi​=Yi​(Si​,Ri​)

The AMCE the average change, switching salary only:

τS=E[Yi(1,Ri)−Yi(0,Ri)]=0.33\tau_S=E\bigl[Y_i(1,R_i)-Y_i(0,R_i)\bigr]=\hl{0.33}τS​=E[Yi​(1,Ri​)−Yi​(0,Ri​)]=0.33

147 of 200 offers accept at a high salary, 81 at a low one: 0.735−0.4050.735-0.4050.735−0.405. Only the 66 that flip move the average: 66/20066/20066/200.

A target like a true β\betaβ, fixed before any data; unlike β\betaβ, it needs no model.

The design's mix of remote work sets its weights: τS=∑rp(r) Δr=12(0.33)+12(0.33)\tau_S=\sum_r p(r)\,\Delta_r=\tfrac12(0.33)+\tfrac12(0.33)τS​=∑r​p(r)Δr​=21​(0.33)+21​(0.33), where Δr\Delta_rΔr​ is the salary effect at remote level rrr.

What exactly is the number we want? Imagine every offer has two answers: the one it would get with a high salary and the one it would get with a low salary, remote work left as the design drew it. These are potential answers, written Y i of one and Y i of zero. What we record is the one that matches the salary actually shown; the other is never seen.

(Widget.) Each dot is one offer. Its left half is the answer with a low salary, its right half the answer with a high salary; filled means accept. Sorted by those two answers, the 200 offers come in three kinds: 81 accept either way, 66 accept only with a high salary, 53 never accept.

(Step.) The AMCE switches salary only and averages the change. At a high salary 147 of 200 accept, 0.735; at a low salary 81, 0.405; the change is 0.33. Put differently, only the 66 offers whose answer flips move the average: 66 over 200.

(Step.) So the AMCE is a target, the same kind of object as the true beta of a textbook regression: fixed before any data, never seen directly. The difference is that beta lives inside a model, while the AMCE is defined by the potential answers alone. Remote work enters only through the design's mix: the AMCE is the salary effect for office offers and for remote offers, weighted by how often the design shows each, a half and a half here. The formal definition and the three assumptions behind it are in D7.

直觉：每份 offer 都有两个“如果”的答案：给高薪会怎样答、给低薪会怎样答，我们只看得到其中一个。AMCE 是只换薪水时答案平均变了多少：200 份里只有 66 份会因为薪水改变答案，所以是 0.33。它像课本里的真实 β 一样是个目标，但不需要任何模型。

Randomisation gives both groups the same mix, seen or unseen

Randomisation a draw that ignores the evaluator and the other attributes sets each level, with known chances above zero.

Same mix of the three kinds, even of tastes nobody records, so the low group stands in for the high group's unseen half:

E[Yi(0,Ri)∣Si=1]=E[Yi(0,Ri)∣Si=0]E[Y_i(0,R_i)\mid S_i=1]=E[Y_i(0,R_i)\mid S_i=0]E[Yi​(0,Ri​)∣Si​=1]=E[Yi​(0,Ri​)∣Si​=0]

So the difference in means is the AMCE, with no model:

yˉ1−yˉ0=0.735−0.405=0.33=τS\bar y_1-\bar y_0=0.735-0.405=\hl{0.33}=\tau_Syˉ​1​−yˉ​0​=0.735−0.405=0.33=τS​

OLS and DID (difference-in-differences) need the same stand-in and assume it is fair: E[εi∣xi]=0E[\varepsilon_i\mid x_i]=0E[εi​∣xi​]=0, parallel trends. Randomisation makes it fair by design.

How do we get the same mix in practice? Randomisation: a draw that has nothing to do with the evaluator and nothing to do with the other attributes sets each level, with chances known in advance and above zero. A coin or a computer's random number is one way to make the draw; the draw is the point, not the coin. (Widget.) The same 200 offers as on the last page: the draw has already sent exactly 100 to each salary.

(Step.) Because it ignores who will answer, both groups get about the same mix of the three kinds, and the same mix of remote work, even though nobody recorded anyone's taste. That makes the low-salary group a fair stand-in for what the high-salary group would have answered with a low salary: on average, the missing half equals the other group's seen half.

(Step.) Only the drawn half is ever seen. High-salary acceptance minus low-salary acceptance lands near 0.33; in the population it is 0.735 minus 0.405, exactly 0.33. No regression, no model. Draw again: it moves a little and stays close. Switch to Not random: eager evaluators end up with the high salary more often, the high group is full of people who accept anything, and the same subtraction comes out far too big.

(Step.) The same problem sits under the methods you already use: the unseen answer needs a stand-in. OLS (ordinary least squares) on observational data assumes the error has mean zero given the regressors; DID (difference-in-differences) assumes parallel trends. Randomisation does not assume the stand-in is fair; the design makes it fair. The proof is in D8.

直觉：随机化是一种和评价者无关、也和其他属性无关的抽签机制，概率事先知道；硬币只是实现方式之一。抽签不看人，所以两组里“怎么都接受、高薪才接受、都不接受”三种人的比例差不多，连没人记录的口味也一样。于是低薪组的平均可以替高薪组补上看不到的另一半答案，均值差就是 AMCE。OLS 和 DID 也要找替身，但靠假设担保；随机化靠设计担保。

The AMCE is the average jump; the additive slope reads it directly

World H invented: a high salary adds 0.50 to office offers and 0.10 to remote ones; half the offers are remote.

τS=12(0.50)+12(0.10)=0.30\tau_S=\tfrac12(0.50)+\tfrac12(0.10)=0.30τS​=21​(0.50)+21​(0.10)=0.30

Additive one slope for both rows

yi=b0+bS Si+bR Riy_i=b_0+\nv{b_S}\,S_i+b_R\,R_iyi​=b0​+bS​Si​+bR​Ri​

It misses every cell by 0.10, yet with randomised attributes bS=0.30=τS\nv{b_S}=0.30=\tau_SbS​=0.30=τS​ (Hainmueller et al. 2014).

Interaction each row its own slope

yi=b0+bS Si+bR Ri+bSR SiRiy_i=b_0+\hl{b_S}\,S_i+b_R\,R_i+b_{SR}\,S_iR_iyi​=b0​+bS​Si​+bR​Ri​+bSR​Si​Ri​

It fits every cell, but bS=0.50\hl{b_S}=0.50bS​=0.50 is the office row only, and bSR=−0.40b_{SR}=-0.40bSR​=−0.40. Averaging the rows, bS+12bSRb_S+\tfrac12 b_{SR}bS​+21​bSR​, gives back 0.30 (Stata: margins).

Now a regression. To see what its coefficient does with the AMCE, take a world where salary matters more for some offers than for others. World H is invented: a high salary lifts office offers by 0.50 but remote offers by only 0.10. Half the offers are remote, so the AMCE is the average jump: half of 0.50 plus half of 0.10, 0.30. (Widget.) The bars on the right are the two rises, drawn to the same scale as the lines.

(Step.) The additive regression, b zero plus b S times S plus b R times R, allows one slope only, so it draws two parallel lines. It misses every cell by 0.10, yet its slope b S is 0.30, exactly the AMCE. That is the result of Hainmueller, Hopkins and Yamamoto: with randomised attributes the additive regression estimates the AMCE even when the model is wrong.

(Step.) The interaction regression adds b S R times S times R, which is one only for high-salary remote offers. Now each row has its own slope and every cell fits. But b S has changed meaning: it is the office row's jump, 0.50. The remote row's jump is b S plus b S R, 0.10, so b S R is minus 0.40. To get the AMCE back, average the rows with the design's weights, b S plus half of b S R; that is what margins does after the regression. Without randomisation even the additive b S is a different average: OLS weights each row by its size times its variance of salary (Angrist and Pischke). Switch to our example: no interaction, the lines are parallel, and every reading is 0.33.

直觉：世界 H 里高薪让坐班的 offer 多 0.50，让远程的只多 0.10，AMCE 是两行跳幅的平均 0.30。加性模型只许一条斜率，画出两条平行线，每格都差 0.10，斜率 b_S 却正好是 0.30；交互模型每格都对，可它的 b_S 只是坐班那一行的 0.50。同一个字母，两种意思。

What the AMCE does not tell you

One design's answer with an interaction, the share of remote offers π\piπ sets the weights:

τS(π)=π Δ1+(1−π) Δ0\tau_S(\pi)=\pi\,\Delta_1+(1-\pi)\,\Delta_0τS​(π)=πΔ1​+(1−π)Δ0​

World H: 0.42, 0.30 or 0.18 at π=0.2\pi=0.2π=0.2, 0.50.50.5, 0.80.80.8; ours stays 0.33. Report π\piπ with every AMCE.

Not a vote a net balance of answers that flip each way:

τS=Pr⁡(flip to accept)−Pr⁡(flip to decline)\tau_S=\Pr(\text{flip to accept})-\Pr(\text{flip to decline})τS​=Pr(flip to accept)−Pr(flip to decline)

33% flipping to accept and none the other way, or 66.5% and 33.5%: both give 0.33.

Not a subgroup gap to compare two groups, compare marginal means, the acceptance rate at each level.

Ours: MM(1)=0.735\mathrm{MM}(1)=0.735MM(1)=0.735, MM(0)=0.405\mathrm{MM}(0)=0.405MM(0)=0.405. A gap between two AMCEs also carries the reference level (D10).

Three things the AMCE does not tell you. First, it is one design's answer. Write pi for the share of remote profiles in the design. The AMCE is a straight line in pi with slope Delta one minus Delta zero. (Widget.) In world H salary matters little for remote jobs, 0.10, and a lot for office jobs, 0.50. Drag pi: 0.42 at 0.2, 0.30 at one half, 0.18 at 0.8. Same people, three different effects of salary, set only by how often the researcher showed remote offers. In our additive data the line is flat at 0.33, a property of the example, not of conjoint experiments. De la Cuesta, Egami and Imai: match the design to a target population, by design or by reweighting; either way report pi.

(Step.) Second, it is not a vote. For one answer the salary effect is plus one, zero or minus one, so the AMCE is the share flipping towards accepting minus the share flipping against. Thirty-three percent flipping one way gives 0.33; so does 66.5 percent one way and 33.5 the other. So say "high salary raises the average acceptance probability by 0.33", never "most respondents prefer a high salary" (Abramson, Koçak and Magazinnik).

(Step.) Third, subgroups. A marginal mean is the acceptance rate at one level, averaged over the design's mix: 0.735 for high salary, 0.405 for low. A gap between two subgroups' AMCEs also contains how the groups treat the reference level, so compare marginal means instead (Leeper, Hobolt and Tilley). D9 and D10 have the details.

直觉：AMCE 是按实验里各种 offer 出现的比例加权平均出来的，有交互时比例一变它就变，所以要报告设计比例；它是净差额，不是投票的票数；比较两群人时，先看每个水平各自的边际均值，别直接拿两个 AMCE 相减。

OLS computes the AMCE; only the design makes it causal

OLS, ordinary least squares. Use it when the effect you want is a difference and the mean is close to a straight line.

Model yi=xi⊤β+εiy_i=x_i^\top\beta+\varepsilon_iyi​=xi⊤​β+εi​

A straight line plus an error. OLS picks the line y^i=xi⊤b\hat y_i=x_i^\top by^​i​=xi⊤​b with the smallest squared misses.

Solves ∑ixi (yi−xi⊤b)=0\sum_i x_i\,\bigl(y_i-\hl{x_i^\top b}\bigr)=0∑i​xi​(yi​−xi⊤​b)=0

The one equation, first appearance: weight 1, a straight-line mean.

Assumes E[εi∣xi]=0E[\varepsilon_i\mid x_i]=0E[εi​∣xi​]=0 (A5): the error averages zero at every xxx.

With salary alone, bbb is the difference in means: under the shuffle, the AMCE, 0.33.

Breaks when nobody shuffles: salary alone gives 0.55=0.33+0.6667×0.330.55=0.33+0.6667\times0.330.55=0.33+0.6667×0.33.

Controlling for remote restores 0.33 only if salary is as good as random within each remote group: an assumption, not a fact.

In practice regress y x controls, vce(cluster id); say which design, controls or fixed effects make E[εi∣xi]=0E[\varepsilon_i\mid x_i]=0E[εi​∣xi​]=0 believable.

OLS (ordinary least squares) is the default tool when the effect you want is a difference and the mean is close to a straight line; for a yes or no outcome that is the linear probability model. Start with the model: y is a straight line in x plus an error. OLS chooses b, the line that makes the squared prediction errors as small as possible. (Step.) Its first-order condition is the next line: every regressor times its residual adds up to zero, so nothing linear in x is left in the error. Keep this equation in mind. It is the one equation, here with weight one and a straight-line mean, and every tool after this changes one piece of it.

(Step.) What must hold for b to be the number you want? The error averages zero at every x. With salary as the only regressor, b is just the difference in means, so under the shuffle OLS returns the AMCE, 0.33.

(Step, then the slider.) Now let nobody shuffle. Drag towards 83 percent: high-salary offers are mostly remote, and the regression on salary alone drifts to 0.55, which is 0.33 plus two thirds of 0.33, the omitted-variable identity. Controlling for remote brings back 0.33, but only because within each remote group salary was as good as random. In real data that is an assumption. The regression computes; the design decides what the number means.

(Step.) How to use it: regress with the controls your design needs and cluster by the unit that repeats; with person or firm fixed effects it is the same equation after taking out each unit's mean. The part you must write in the paper is why the error averages zero given what you control for. The derivations are in D11 to D13.

直觉：OLS 用在“要的是差、平均值接近直线”的时候。它让残差和每个解释变量都不相关；在抽签的数据里，它算出的正好是 AMCE。没人抽签时，同一条命令会给出 0.55，回归自己不会告诉你哪个数是对的。

Standard errors answer only the third question

SE, standard error. Choose it by how the data were sampled: cluster by the unit that repeats, a person or a firm.

Same estimate Var⁡(b)=(X⊤X)−1 B (X⊤X)−1\operatorname{Var}(b)=(X^\top X)^{-1}\,\hl{B}\,(X^\top X)^{-1}Var(b)=(X⊤X)−1B(X⊤X)−1

bbb never changes; only the middle, BBB, does. It holds what you assume about sampling and grouping.

Assumes

  • textbook: equal noise, no correlation (A6, A7)
  • HC1 (heteroskedasticity-consistent, version 1): independent answers
  • CR1 (cluster-robust, version 1): independent people, and many of them

A6 fails a yes or no answer has variance p(1−p)p(1-p)p(1−p): the LPM (linear probability model) is heteroskedastic by construction.

Observational SE: 0.0305 to 0.0369.

A7 fails one person's six answers share a tendency, but salary was shuffled within person.

Clustering adds little: 0.0369 to 0.0385.

Whatever tool you pick, you also pick a standard error, and the rule is short: choose it by how the data were sampled and grouped, and cluster by the unit that repeats, a respondent here, a firm in a panel. Changing the standard error never changes b. Every version keeps the same estimate and changes only the middle of the sandwich, B, which is where your assumptions about sampling and grouping sit. The textbook formula assumes every answer is equally noisy and no two are correlated. HC1, White's heteroskedasticity-consistent version, only assumes the answers are independent. CR1, cluster-robust, only assumes the people are independent, and that there are many of them.

(Step.) A6 fails by construction here: a yes or no answer has variance p times one minus p, which differs from cell to cell. In the observational design the robust SE (standard error) jumps from 0.0305 to 0.0369, because the offers that identify salary sit in the noisiest cells.

(Step.) A7 fails inside each person: six answers share a personal tendency. But salary was shuffled within person, so clustering adds little, 0.0369 to 0.0385. Compare only the first and the last number and you would credit clustering with what heteroskedasticity did. The dot never moves: 0.33 under every layer. Details in D14 to D16.

直觉：标准误按数据怎么抽、怎么分组来选，按重复出现的单位（人、公司）聚类。它只回答“有多大把握”，估计值 0.33 一动不动；观察设计里标准误的跳升主要来自异方差，聚类只多加了一点点。

GLS buys precision by believing more about the errors

GLS, generalized least squares, here random effects. Use it when one unit's errors move together and you can model how.

Solves ∑gXg⊤ Ωg−1 (yg−Xgβ)=0\sum_g X_g^\top\,\hl{\Omega_g^{-1}}\,\bigl(y_g-X_g\beta\bigr)=0∑g​Xg⊤​Ωg−1​(yg​−Xg​β)=0

A new weight: one block per unit. Random effects: subtract θ\thetaθ times each unit's mean, then OLS (θ=0\theta=0θ=0 pooled OLS, θ=1\theta=1θ=1 fixed effects).

Assumes a person's tendency to accept, cgc_gcg​, is unrelated to the offers they saw: E[cg∣Xg]=0E[c_g\mid X_g]=0E[cg​∣Xg​]=0.

Plus strict exogeneity of every answer; for the smaller standard error, the right Ω\OmegaΩ.

Breaks when the tendency tracks the offers: GLS is inconsistent, fixed effects survives. A conjoint rules this out by design.

In practice xtreg y x, re vce(cluster id), then Mundlak's check; if it fails, xtreg y x, fe.

Ours: θ=0.4151\theta=0.4151θ=0.4151; 0.3241 (SE 0.0232) against OLS 0.3300 (SE 0.0240).

When do you reach for GLS (generalized least squares)? When the errors of one unit move together, a person's six answers or a firm's ten years, and you are willing to model how. It changes the weight in the one equation: instead of one per row, one block per unit, the inverse of the covariance of its errors. For random effects this comes down to one number, theta: subtract theta times each unit's own mean from every answer and every regressor, then run OLS. Theta zero is pooled OLS, theta one is fixed effects; ours is 0.4151. (Sliders: theta grows with the correlation between one person's answers and with the number of answers.)

(Step.) The price is an assumption: a person's general tendency to accept must be unrelated to the offers they saw. (Step.) A conjoint guarantees it, because the random device deals offers without looking at the person. With real job seekers it is a bet: the more employable may get better offers and also accept more. If it fails, GLS is inconsistent and only fixed effects survives. In firm panels this is the usual case: a well-run firm differs in ways that also move its regressors.

(Step.) How to use it: random effects with cluster-robust standard errors, then Mundlak's check, adding each unit's average regressors; if those matter, use fixed effects. In our data GLS gives 0.3241 with a standard error of 0.0232, against 0.3300 and 0.0240 for OLS: the same target, a little more precise. The derivation is in D17 to D19.

直觉：GLS 用在“同一个单位的误差连在一起，而且你愿意给它建模”的时候。它多相信一点“误差长什么样”，换来更小的标准误；代价是要相信单位自己的特质和解释变量无关。随机实验白送这个假设，公司面板里通常要用固定效应。

Logit changes the shape, so its effect is an odds ratio

Logit, logistic regression, fitted by maximum likelihood. Use it for a yes or no outcome when fitted probabilities must stay between 0 and 1.

Solves ∑ixi (yi−Λ(xi⊤β))=0\sum_i x_i\,\bigl(y_i-\hl{\Lambda(x_i^\top\beta)}\bigr)=0∑i​xi​(yi​−Λ(xi⊤​β))=0

The score (the gradient of log⁡L\log LlogL): the one equation with an S-shaped mean, weight 1.

Assumes one odds ratio fits every stratum.

Ours does not: the same +0.33 is an OR (odds ratio) of 4.20 for office jobs, 6.79 for remote ones.

Breaks when the shape is wrong: logit reports a compromise set by the design, OR 5.0995.

Without remote it reads 4.0748: odds ratios do not average, so that is a different number, not a bias.

In practice logit y x, vce(cluster id), then margins, dydx(x): report the AME (average marginal effect), here 0.3300, the difference in means under exact balance.

(Maximum likelihood itself was covered in an earlier session; the words "maximum likelihood" on this slide link to its slides.)

Logit is the tool for a yes or no outcome when fitted probabilities must stay between zero and one: accept or not here, default or not, pay a dividend or not in firm data. It keeps the weights and changes the shape: the mean is an S-curve. Its score, the gradient of the log-likelihood, is again the one equation with weight one. If the shape is right, the maximum likelihood estimator is consistent and asymptotically efficient; it is not unbiased.

(Step.) What you must assume is that one odds ratio describes the effect in every stratum. Ours does not: the same plus 0.33 in probability is an odds ratio of 4.20 for office jobs and 6.79 for remote ones, because the second step climbs the flat top of the S. (Step, sliders.) So logit reports a compromise set by the design, 5.0995. Drop remote and it reads 4.0748: odds ratios do not average, even with no confounding at all. That is a different number, not a bias.

(Step.) How to use it: run the logit with clustered standard errors, then margins, and report the AME (average marginal effect), the average change in the fitted probability. Under exact balance it equals the difference in means, 0.33, even with the wrong shape. The proofs and the likelihood surface are in D20 to D24.

直觉：logit 用在 0/1 结果、需要拟合概率落在 0 到 1 之间的时候。它把直线换成 S 形曲线，说话用的是优势比（odds ratio）；真相不按优势比走时，它只能给一个由设计决定的折中值。报告时换回概率，用平均边际效应。

PPML reports how many times, not how many more

PPML, Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood. Use it for a non-negative outcome with proportional effects, zeros included.

Target the AMCE's two means, as a ratio:

E[Yi(1,Ri)]E[Yi(0,Ri)]=0.7350.405=1.8148\dfrac{E[Y_i(1,R_i)]}{E[Y_i(0,R_i)]}=\dfrac{0.735}{0.405}=\hl{1.8148}E[Yi​(0,Ri​)]E[Yi​(1,Ri​)]​=0.4050.735​=1.8148

A high salary raises acceptance by 81.5%. Their difference, 0.33, is the AMCE.

Model an exponential mean, so effects multiply:

μi=exp⁡(β0+βSSi+βRRi)=eβ0 (eβS)Si (eβR)Ri\mu_i=\exp(\beta_0+\beta_SS_i+\beta_RR_i)=e^{\beta_0}\,(e^{\beta_S})^{S_i}\,(e^{\beta_R})^{R_i}μi​=exp(β0​+βS​Si​+βR​Ri​)=eβ0​(eβS​)Si​(eβR​)Ri​

eβSe^{\beta_S}eβS​: the factor a high salary multiplies by, the same in every row.

Our truth adds +0.33 in both rows is ×2.375\times2.375×2.375 for office and ×1.579\times1.579×1.579 for remote offers. World M multiplies: ×2.00\times2.00×2.00 in both.

World M is invented, to show what PPML's model looks like when it is right.

PPML (Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood) is the tool for a non-negative outcome where effects are proportional: counts, sales, trade flows, patents, likes, often with many zeros. Start from the target. It is built from the same two means as the AMCE: the acceptance rate if every offer had a high salary, 0.735, and if every offer had a low one, 0.405. The AMCE is their difference, 0.33; PPML's target is their ratio, 1.8148: a high salary raises acceptance by 81.5 percent.

(Step.) The model behind it is an exponential mean. Because the exponential of a sum is a product, the mean factorises: a baseline, times e to the beta S if the salary is high, times e to the beta R if the offer is remote. So e to the beta S is the factor a high salary multiplies by, the same in every row.

(Step.) Our truth does not work that way. It adds 0.33 in both rows, which is times 2.375 for office offers and times 1.579 for remote ones. (Widget.) On the difference scale our two rows rise in parallel; on the ratio scale, a log axis, they do not. World M is invented to show the opposite case, the one PPML's model describes: 0.20 to 0.40 and 0.35 to 0.70, times 2.00 in both rows, parallel on the ratio scale. Keep both pictures: on the next page PPML still returns exactly 0.735 over 0.405 in our data, and later we see what happens when the design is not randomised. Derivations: D25 to D27.

直觉：PPML 用在非负、效应按比例的结果上（计数、销售额、贸易额、点赞数），零很多也没关系。它要的数和 AMCE 用的是同一对均值：AMCE 取差，0.33；PPML 取比，1.8148，也就是高 81.5%。它的模型是指数均值，所以效应是乘出来的：e^βS 就是高薪在每一行都乘上的那个倍数。课上的真值是“加”出来的，世界 M 才是“乘”出来的。

PPML's equation is a set of totals that must match

Solves Poisson's score equation, one row per regressor in xi=(1,Si,Ri)⊤x_i=(1,S_i,R_i)^\topxi​=(1,Si​,Ri​)⊤:

∑ixi (yi−μ^i)=0,μ^i=exp⁡(xi⊤β^)\sum_i x_i\,\bigl(y_i-\hat\mu_i\bigr)=0,\qquad \hat\mu_i=\exp(x_i^\top\hat\beta)∑i​xi​(yi​−μ^​i​)=0,μ^​i​=exp(xi⊤​β^​)

Totals fitted acceptances add up to the observed ones: over all offers, the high-salary ones, the remote ones.

684, 441 and 441. Cell by cell they need not match.

Randomised both salary groups are half remote, so the remote factor cancels:

eβ^S=yˉ1/yˉ0=0.735/0.405=1.8148e^{\hat\beta_S}=\bar y_1/\bar y_0=0.735/0.405=\hl{1.8148}eβ^​S​=yˉ​1​/yˉ​0​=0.735/0.405=1.8148

whatever the true mean: the design, not the model, makes it the ratio we want.

Observational the remote factor no longer cancels: the raw ratio 2.8644 is eβ^S=1.8891e^{\hat\beta_S}=1.8891eβ^​S​=1.8891 times a remote imbalance of 1.5163.

How does PPML compute its number? It solves Poisson's score equation, the gradient of the Poisson log-likelihood set to zero: the one equation again, with an exponential mean and weight one. With a constant, salary and remote it has three rows.

(Step.) Read each row as bookkeeping. The constant's row says the fitted acceptances add up to the observed ones over all 1,200 offers: 684. Salary's row says the same over the high-salary offers: 441. Remote's row, over the remote offers: 441. (Widget.) The navy boxes are those three totals; the other two margins follow from them. Inside the cells the fit is off by about 14 acceptances each way, because our truth adds instead of multiplying, and nothing in the equation asks the cells to match.

(Step.) Divide the high-salary total by the low-salary total. The baseline cancels, and with randomisation both salary groups are half remote, so the remote factor cancels too: e to the beta S is exactly 0.735 over 0.405, 1.8148, the risk ratio, whatever the true mean. Zou (2004) calls this modified Poisson regression.

(Step.) Switch the widget to observational. The totals still match, but now five in six high-salary offers are remote and one in six low-salary ones, so the remote factor no longer cancels. The raw ratio, 0.845 over 0.295, is 2.8644; PPML reports 1.8891 and attributes the remaining factor, 1.5163, to the remote imbalance. Whether 1.8891 means anything depends on whether one common ratio describes the truth: ours has 2.375 and 1.579. We return to that on the two-regimes page. The algebra is in D27.

直觉：PPML 的方程就是三本账：拟合的接受数加起来，要在全部 offer、高薪 offer、远程 offer 里各自等于实际的接受数（684、441、441）；每一格对不上没关系。随机化时两组都是一半远程，远程的倍数约掉，e^βS 恰好是 0.735/0.405。观察数据里约不掉，原始比值 2.8644 = 1.8891 × 1.5163。

Only the mean has to be right

Average one row of the equation at the true β∘\beta^\circβ∘, conditioning on xix_ixi​ first:

E[xi(E[yi∣xi]−exi⊤β∘)]E\bigl[x_i\bigl(\hl{E[y_i\mid x_i]-e^{x_i^\top\beta^\circ}}\bigr)\bigr]E[xi​(E[yi​∣xi​]−exi⊤​β∘)]

yiy_iyi​ enters only through its mean.

Mean right if E[y∣x]=exp⁡(x⊤β∘)E[y\mid x]=\exp(x^\top\beta^\circ)E[y∣x]=exp(x⊤β∘), the bracket is zero whatever the variance, the share of zeros, or whether yyy is a count.

So β^\hat\betaβ^​ is consistent, not unbiased (Gourieroux, Monfort & Trognon 1984). The full conditions are in D25.

Pseudo the Poisson likelihood is scaffolding. The variance it implies is wrong, so use robust or clustered standard errors.

Mean wrong the equation still has a root, and nothing flags it.

Why can PPML get away with a Poisson likelihood when our outcome is a yes or no answer? Take one row of the equation and average it at the true value, conditioning on x first. The outcome appears only as y minus its fitted mean, so after conditioning only its mean is left: the red bracket.

(Step.) If the mean is exponential, the bracket is zero at the truth, whatever the variance, the share of zeros, or whether y is a count at all. That is the result of Gourieroux, Monfort and Trognon (1984). It gives consistency, not unbiasedness: the estimate settles on the truth as the sample grows. (Widget.) Four outcomes with the same mean and very different shapes: Poisson counts, a continuous skewed variable, one with forty percent zeros, and a 0/1 answer like ours. Draw 50 more: in every panel the slopes centre on 1. The full list of conditions, including identification and finite moments, is in D25.

(Step.) That is what pseudo means: the Poisson likelihood is scaffolding that produces the equation; what PPML really solves are moment conditions. The variance the scaffolding implies, variance equal to the mean, is wrong for most data, so the default Poisson standard errors are wrong too: use robust or clustered ones.

(Step.) The flip side: if the mean is wrong, the equation still has a root, a pseudo-true value, and nothing in the output flags it.

直觉：方程里 y 只以“y 减均值”出现，先在每个 x 上取平均，就只剩“均值公式对不对”这一件事。所以 y 是不是泊松、是不是整数、零多不多都不要紧，泊松似然只是搭的架子；代价是默认标准误不能用，要用稳健或聚类标准误。均值错了，方程照样有解，而且不会报警。

log-OLS answers a different question

Model y=exp⁡(x⊤β) ηy=\exp(x^\top\beta)\,\etay=exp(x⊤β)η with E[η∣x]=1E[\eta\mid x]=1E[η∣x]=1, so PPML's target is log⁡E[y∣x]=x⊤β\log E[y\mid x]=x^\top\betalogE[y∣x]=x⊤β.

Log first then average, and a term appears:

E[log⁡y∣x]=x⊤β+E[log⁡η∣x]E[\log y\mid x]=x^\top\beta+\hl{E[\log\eta\mid x]}E[logy∣x]=x⊤β+E[logη∣x]

The mean of the logs sits below the log of the mean (Jensen's inequality).

Same slope if and only if E[log⁡η∣x]E[\log\eta\mid x]E[logη∣x] does not move with xxx. Here it falls as the spread grows: slope 1−γ/2=0.701-\gamma/2=0.701−γ/2=0.70 at γ=0.6\gamma=0.6γ=0.6.

Not a bias log-OLS consistently estimates its own target, the slope of E[log⁡y∣x]E[\log y\mid x]E[logy∣x]; the spread matters only through E[log⁡η∣x]E[\log\eta\mid x]E[logη∣x].

Many papers take logs of y and run OLS. A good estimator, of a different estimand. Write the multiplicative model: y is the exponential mean times an error eta whose mean is one at every x. PPML targets the log of the mean, whose slope is beta.

(Step.) Take logs first and average afterwards, and an extra term appears: the mean of log eta. By Jensen's inequality the mean of a log is below the log of the mean, so the term is negative.

(Step.) The two slopes agree if and only if that term does not move with x, for example when eta has the same distribution shape at every x. (Slider.) In the simulation the spread grows with x at rate gamma; the red band, the gap, widens, and the log-OLS target flattens to one minus gamma over two: 0.70 at gamma 0.6, against the true 1. With 20,000 draws log-OLS gave 0.6995, right on its own target, and PPML 0.9807 (D26).

(Step.) So do not say heteroskedasticity makes log-OLS inconsistent. It consistently estimates the slope of the expected log; the variance matters only through the mean of log eta. The question is which number you want.

直觉：先取对数再平均，和先平均再取对数，是两回事；只要 log η 的平均随 x 变，log-OLS 就在回答另一个问题，不是谁算错了。

Zeros: dropping them or adding one changes the target again

The problem log⁡0\log 0log0 is undefined, and many outcomes are often zero: likes, patents, trade.

Drop the zeros the slope among positive yyy only: 0.80 here, where xxx also moves the share of zeros.

Add one log⁡(1+c y)\log(1+c\,y)log(1+cy) depends on the unit ccc of yyy when xxx moves the share of zeros: no unit is the right one (Chen & Roth 2024).

0.75 with c=1c=1c=1, 1.48 with c=100c=100c=100, 2.80 with c=106c=10^6c=106.

PPML keeps yi=0y_i=0yi​=0; rescaling yyy only moves its intercept: 0.99 in every unit.

The second place where a habit changes the target: zeros. The log of zero does not exist, and many outcomes we care about are often zero.

(Step.) Dropping the zeros answers a question about positive outcomes only. In the simulation, where x also lowers the chance of a zero, that slope is 0.80 against a true 1. (Widget.) Switch to zeros unrelated to x and it comes back to 1: whether dropping is harmless depends on the data, not on the method.

(Step.) Adding one before taking logs is worse: the answer depends on the unit of y. Drag c, the unit: measure y in cents instead of pounds and the slope moves from 0.75 to 1.48; in larger units still it reaches 2.80. When x moves the share of zeros, the bigger the unit, the more log of one plus c y measures whether y is positive at all. Chen and Roth (2024) show there is no unit that makes it right. If the share of zeros does not depend on x the drift is much smaller, but it does not vanish.

(Step.) PPML keeps the zeros as they are, and multiplying y by any constant only shifts its intercept: 0.99 in every unit here.

直觉：log 0 没有定义。扔掉零，估的是“正值里面”的效应；加 1 再取对数，答案会随 y 的单位变，而且没有哪个单位是对的。PPML 把零原样留着，换单位只动截距，斜率不变。

Report the ratio with both ends of its interval

In Stata poisson y S R, vce(cluster id) irr, or with many fixed effects ppmlhdfe (Correia et al. 2020).

Cluster by respondent: the default Poisson SE assumes Var⁡(y∣x)=μ\operatorname{Var}(y\mid x)=\muVar(y∣x)=μ.

Log scale symmetric: β^S=0.5960\hat\beta_S=0.5960β^​S​=0.5960 with clustered SE 0.0551, so 0.4880 to 0.7040.

Percent scale exponentiate and subtract one: lopsided.

eβ^S−1=+81.5%e^{\hat\beta_S}-1=+81.5\%eβ^​S​−1=+81.5%, from +62.9%\hl{+62.9\%}+62.9% to +102.2%\hl{+102.2\%}+102.2%

18.6 points below and 20.7 above: write both ends, never “±”.

How to run and report it. In Stata, poisson with clustered standard errors and the irr option, which prints e to the beta; with many fixed effects, ppmlhdfe by Correia, Guimarães and Zylkin. Cluster by the unit that repeats, the respondent here: the default Poisson standard error assumes the variance equals the mean, which a 0/1 answer does not satisfy.

(Step.) On the log scale the interval is symmetric: 0.5960 plus or minus 1.96 times 0.0551, from 0.4880 to 0.7040.

(Step.) Exponentiate and subtract one: plus 81.5 percent, with an interval from plus 62.9 to plus 102.2 percent, 18.6 points below and 20.7 above, lopsided because the exponential is convex. (Slider.) The larger the standard error, the more lopsided. So report the two endpoints, never plus or minus a percentage. The same computation is in D27.

直觉：在对数尺度上区间是对称的，换回百分比后因为指数函数是凸的，右边总比左边长，所以两个端点都要写，不写“±”。默认的泊松标准误假设方差等于均值，要用聚类标准误。

In a published paper: likes are counts, the effect is a percent

The paper Zhang & Zhao (2026), International Journal of Research in Marketing: after a sponsored post, does the next post get less engagement?

271,779 videos from 1,913 influencers.

A rate, linear the like rate falls by 0.27 percentage points, for example from 5% to 4.73% (Table 2).

A count, PPML with many fixed effects (ppmlhdfe): β^=−0.317\hat\beta=-0.317β^​=−0.317, so mean likes change by

e−0.317−1=−27.2%e^{-0.317}-1=\hl{-27.2\%}e−0.317−1=−27.2%

Total engagement: e−0.258−1=−22.7%e^{-0.258}-1=-22.7\%e−0.258−1=−22.7% (Table 4).

Two estimands a difference in a rate and a ratio of mean counts: say which one your number is.

PPML is not an exotic tool. Here it is in a paper presented to this group in February: Zhang and Zhao (2026) in the International Journal of Research in Marketing (the link opens the article). Their question: after an influencer posts sponsored content, does the next, unsponsored post get less engagement? 271,779 videos from 1,913 influencers.

(Step.) Their linear models use the like rate, likes per view, and report the effect in percentage points: 0.27 points, for example from 5 percent to 4.73. That is a difference ruler.

(Step.) For the like count they use Poisson pseudo-likelihood with many fixed effects, ppmlhdfe, the command of Correia, Guimarães and Zylkin (2020). The coefficient is minus 0.317, and they report exactly what we did on the last page: e to the minus 0.317, minus one, a 27.2 percent drop in mean likes; for total engagement, minus 0.258, a 22.7 percent drop. That is a ratio ruler.

(Step.) Same treatment, two estimands: a difference in a rate, and a ratio of mean counts. The two numbers cannot be compared directly, not least because views, the rate's denominator, are an outcome too. The habit to take away: say which estimand your number is, and report a ratio as e to the beta minus one.

直觉：组里的论文就在用 PPML：点赞率用线性模型，答案是“少 0.27 个百分点”；点赞数用 PPML（ppmlhdfe），答案是“均值少 27.2%”，也就是 e^−0.317 − 1。同一个处理、两把尺子、两个估计目标，写论文时要说清楚自己的数是哪一个。

Each estimator is a ruler with its own graduation and weights

OLS (ordinary least squares) graduated in probability points, every answer weight 1. Reads 0.33.

μ=x⊤β\mu=x^\top\betaμ=x⊤β; reads true if E[ε∣x]=0E[\varepsilon\mid x]=0E[ε∣x]=0: the coin

GLS (generalized least squares) same ticks, new weights: one person's six answers count for less than six strangers'.

w=Ω−1w=\Omega^{-1}w=Ω−1: 0.324, SE 0.0232 against 0.0240; needs E[cg∣Xg]=0E[c_g\mid X_g]=0E[cg​∣Xg​]=0

Logit graduated in log-odds. Reads 1.40, odds ×\times×4.07; hold remote fixed and it reads 1.63, ×\times×5.10.

μ=Λ(x⊤β)\mu=\Lambda(x^\top\beta)μ=Λ(x⊤β); back on the first ruler: AME (average marginal effect) 0.33

PPML (Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood) graduated in logs. Reads 0.596, a ratio of ×\times×1.81.

μ=exp⁡(x⊤β)\mu=\exp(x^\top\beta)μ=exp(x⊤β); needs the mean right (plus identification, moments, independent draws), not a Poisson yyy

All four solve ∑ixi wi (yi−μi)=0\sum_i x_i\,w_i\,(y_i-\mu_i)=0∑i​xi​wi​(yi​−μi​)=0: graduation μ\muμ, weights www, and the condition under which the reading is true.

The tools of this talk are different rulers laid on the same table: the gap between the acceptance rate under a low salary, 0.405, and under a high one, 0.735. OLS (ordinary least squares) is graduated in probability points and counts every answer once. It reads 0.33 directly, and the reading is true when the error averages zero at every x, which the coin guarantees.

(Step.) GLS (generalized least squares) keeps the ticks but changes the weights: one person's six answers share a personal tendency, so together they count for less than six answers from six strangers. It reads 0.324 and is a little steadier, standard error 0.0232 against 0.0240 for OLS. The price is an assumption: a person's tendency must be unrelated to the offers they saw.

(Step.) Logit is graduated in log-odds: watch the ticks crowd together near zero and one. The same gap reads 1.40, an odds ratio of 4.07. Hold remote fixed and the reading becomes 1.63, an odds ratio of 5.10: the unit itself depends on what else is in the model. That is non-collapsibility, and it is why we convert back to the first ruler, the AME (average marginal effect), which is 0.33 again.

(Step.) PPML (Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood) is graduated in logs, with the ticks crowding towards zero instead. It reads 0.596, a ratio of 1.81: a high salary raises acceptance by about 81 percent. The reading is true as long as the mean is exponential, plus identification, finite moments and independent sampling; the outcome need not be Poisson, or even a count.

(Step.) So every ruler solves the one equation from the title slide. The graduation is the shape of the mean, mu; the weights are w; and the third dial is the condition under which the reading is true. Converted back to probability points, all four agree on about 0.33. We have now met each of these rulers one at a time; next, the equation they share.

直觉：同一张桌子（高薪和低薪的接受率之差），换不同的尺子量。OLS 是等距刻度，读 0.33。GLS 刻度不变，但给读数加权：同一个人的六个回答不算六个独立读数。logit 是对数优势刻度，读 1.40，也就是优势比 4.07；控制远程以后读 1.63（优势比 5.10），单位会随模型里放了什么而变。PPML 是对数刻度，读 0.596，也就是 1.81 倍。要比较，先换算回概率：都在 0.33 左右。尺子之间的区别就是三个旋钮：刻度（μ 的形状）、权重 w、读数在什么条件下为真。

Underneath, all five solve one equation

So choosing a tool means turning three dials, and your data, not taste, sets each one.

∑ixi wi (yi−μi)=0\sum_i x_i\,\nv{w_i}\,\bigl(y_i-\hl{\mu_i}\bigr)=0i∑​xi​wi​(yi​−μi​)=0

Shape of μ\muμ set by the outcome: a line for a difference (AMCE, OLS, GLS), an S-curve for yes or no (logit), an exponential for proportional effects (PPML)

Weight www set by the errors: 1, or one block per unit if you can model them (GLS)

Must hold the mean, and for a causal reading the design behind it: the assumption each tool spends

Uncertainty set by the sampling: one sandwich, V=A−1BA−1V=A^{-1}BA^{-1}V=A−1BA−1, with BBB built from the units that repeat

Put the tools side by side and they solve one equation: each regressor, times a weight, times the gap between the answer and the fitted mean, adds up to zero. So choosing a tool means turning three dials, and your data set each one. The shape of the mean is set by the outcome: a line when the effect you want is a difference, an S-curve for a yes or no outcome, an exponential for proportional effects. The weight is set by the errors: one, or a block per unit if you can model how a unit's errors move together.

(Toggle.) Click through in the order of the talk. The bottom line is what has to hold for the equation to average zero at the truth: that is the assumption each tool spends. (Step.) And the standard error is set by the sampling: one sandwich, A inverse B A inverse, where the bread A comes from the tool and the meat B from how the data were sampled and grouped. Every argument about which standard error to report is an argument about B.

The derivation from the likelihood, the sandwich, the full table of assumptions and six common misreadings are in D28 to D31.

直觉：五件工具底下是同一个方程，挑工具就是拧三个旋钮：结果变量的样子决定均值形状，误差的结构决定权重，数据怎么抽决定标准误。每拧一次，都在选你要相信的东西。

Changing the estimator changes what you assume

Same four acceptance rates in both columns (0.90, 0.57, 0.57, 0.24); only where the rows sit changes (300 each, or 500/100/100/500).

Salary effectRandomisedObservational
OLS, salary only0.33000.5500
OLS, salary and remote0.33000.3300
GLS, random effects0.32410.3383
Logit odds ratio5.09955.2247
Logit AME0.33000.3300
PPML ratio1.81481.8891

GLS targets the same 0.33 and differs only by sampling noise (cluster SE 0.0232 and 0.0351). The observational AME is 0.33 only because this example is symmetric (500/100/100/500 and equal off-diagonal rates).

Randomised: the design identifies; the estimator only picks the scale and the standard error.
Observational: the functional form becomes part of the identification.

The same is true of difference-in-differences: whether parallel trends holds can depend on the scale of the outcome (Roth & Sant'Anna 2023).

This is where the talk lands, and for those of us who work with observational data, firm panels or archives, it is the slide to remember. Every estimator in both designs; the four true acceptance rates are identical in the two columns, only where the rows sit has changed.

OLS with remote controlled stays at 0.33, because the truth really is one common difference. Logit assumes one common odds ratio, but the strata have 4.20 and 6.79, so it reports a compromise, and the compromise moves from 5.0995 to 5.2247 when the design moves. PPML does the same on the ratio scale, 1.8148 to 1.8891; the strata swap sides, because remote has the larger odds ratio but the smaller ratio. The design sets the weights of each compromise (for OLS, the familiar variance weighting of a saturated control: Angrist and Pischke 2009, section 3.3.1). GLS moves too, but only by sampling noise around 0.33.

So under randomisation, choosing OLS or logit is choosing a reporting scale and a standard error. In observational data it is choosing an identifying assumption, the point Roth and Sant'Anna make for parallel trends.

直觉：随机化时，设计已经把要的数钉住，估计量只决定用什么尺度汇报、标准误怎么算；观察数据里，选 OLS、logit 还是 PPML，等于选“各层的差、OR（odds ratio，优势比）还是比值相同”，这本身就是识别假设。

Three questions to take back to your own research

1

Take the main assumption in your current project. Which question does it serve: what number you want, how you compute it, or how sure you are?

2

If you reported your main effect as a ratio or an odds ratio instead of a difference, would your conclusion change?And would your identifying assumption change with it?

3

When a reader asks “why should I believe it?”, where does your answer come from?The design, a model of the outcome, or the way the data were collected?

Let us stop the mathematics here. These three questions need no econometrics at all; anyone in the room can answer them about their own work, whether it is a survey, an experiment, interviews coded into numbers, or archival data.

Give people a minute and a half in pairs, then ask two people to share: about three minutes in all. For the first question, push gently: if your key assumption failed, would the number be wrong, or only its uncertainty? For the second: many effects in our fields are naturally read as ratios, for sales, citations or counts of events, and the scale you report the effect on is a choice. For the third: notice whether the answer is “because we randomised”, “because the model is right”, or “because the sample is large”.

直觉：不用公式，只问自己：我的主要假设在回答哪一个问题？换个尺度，结论还站得住吗？别人问“凭什么信”，我的底气来自设计、模型，还是数据的来路？

This is the list from the 2024 foundations session, linked in the title: the classical linear regression model in eight assumptions. The first three are about the model and the data, the last five are about the error term.

(Show the matrix.) Homoskedasticity and no autocorrelation are easiest to remember as one picture: the covariance matrix of the errors has the same number, sigma squared, all along the diagonal, and zeros everywhere else. That picture is what gives the familiar variance formula, sigma squared times X-transpose-X inverse.

(Closing line.) In 2024 we asked: if I believe these, what does OLS give me? Today the question is different: which tool, when, and what does each one ask you to assume? Page 3 sorts the same eight by the question each one answers; the next two slides stack them into levels, from strongest to weakest.

OLS assumptions: the levels, from strongest to weakest

From the foundations session two years ago; the frameworks follow Wooldridge (2020), Introductory Econometrics. Each box relaxes one thing in the box above (red). Click a box.

Strongest · cross-section
Textbook Wooldridge (2020), ch. 4: its assumptions MLR.1 to MLR.6
A1 to A5linear mean, full rank, random sampling, E(εi∣X)=0E(\varepsilon_i\mid X)=0E(εi​∣X)=0no omitted variable, no reverse causality

You get OLS is BLUE (best linear unbiased estimator), and ttt and FFF tests are exact in any sample size, even N=20N=20N=20.

Use it when the sample is small and normal errors are credible. Rare in practice.

2 · Gauss–Markov

= CLM without normality
Textbook Wooldridge (2020), ch. 3: MLR.1 to MLR.5 and the Gauss–Markov theorem
A1 to A7as in the CLM
A8normality droppederrors may have any distribution
You get OLS is BLUE: the smallest variance among linear unbiased estimators. This is the Gauss–Markov theorem itself; normality was never part of it. Tests are valid only approximately, in large samples (CLT, central limit theorem).

Use it when the sample is reasonably large and the textbook standard error is believable: equal noise, independent rows.

3 · Large-sample OLS

= Gauss–Markov without homoskedasticity
Textbook Wooldridge (2020), ch. 5 (large samples) and ch. 8 (robust inference)
A1 to A5as above: the mean is right and the rows are independent
A6homoskedasticity droppedeach row may have its own error variance
You get OLS is still unbiased and consistent, but no longer BLUE. The textbook standard error is wrong: use a robust one, HC1 (heteroskedasticity-consistent; White 1980), or model the variance with GLS.

Use it when you have a cross-section: the modern default. A yes or no outcome always lands here (page 12: 0.0305 becomes 0.0369).

4a · Time series Gauss–Markov

Random sampling replaced
Textbook Wooldridge (2020), ch. 10: TS.1 to TS.6
A3no longer independent draws: today depends on yesterday
A5E(εt∣X)=0E(\varepsilon_t\mid X)=0E(εt​∣X)=0 with XXX from all periodsstrict exogeneity: stronger than in a cross-section

You get OLS is BLUE; add normal errors and the tests are exact again.

Use it when no lagged outcome is a regressor: strict exogeneity rules out yt−1y_{t-1}yt−1​.

4b · Time series, large sample

Strict exogeneity relaxed to the current period
Textbook Wooldridge (2020), ch. 11: TS.1′ to TS.5′; HAC standard errors in ch. 12
A3stationary and weakly dependentthe series does not drift; distant periods are nearly unrelated
A5E(εt∣xt)=0E(\varepsilon_t\mid x_t)=0E(εt​∣xt​)=0only the current regressors; yt−1y_{t-1}yt−1​ allowed

You get OLS is consistent and asymptotically normal, but may be biased in a finite sample. Use a HAC (heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent) standard error, such as Newey–West.

Use it when the model has a lagged outcome, as most macro models do. A non-stationary series fits neither 4a nor 4b: difference it or model cointegration.

You get demeaning within each unit removes cgc_gcg​, so bbb is consistent even when cgc_gcg​ is related to XXX. The price: no effect of anything that never changes within a unit.

Use it when the unit's own tendency may track the regressors: a firm's quality and its spending, say. The safe default for firm panels.

+E(cg∣Xg)=0E(c_g\mid X_g)=0E(cg​∣Xg​)=0the unit's tendency is unrelated to its regressors
You get GLS with one number, θ\thetaθ (page 13): more precise than FE, and effects of time-invariant regressors. If E(cg∣Xg)≠0E(c_g\mid X_g)\neq 0E(cg​∣Xg​)=0, RE is inconsistent.

Use it when the design guarantees it, as a conjoint does: 200 people × 6 answers is a short panel. Otherwise test it: Hausman, or its cluster-robust version, Mundlak's regression; reject, and use FE.

This page comes from the foundations session two years ago; the slides are linked at the top. The frameworks and their labels follow Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics; each card gives the chapter, and the book numbers the assumptions in its own way (MLR, TS). The same eight assumptions can be packaged into frameworks, from the strongest to the weakest. Each box relaxes one thing in the box above.

The classical linear model takes all eight and gives exact tests in any sample. Drop normality and you are in Gauss–Markov: OLS is still BLUE, tests become large-sample approximations. Drop homoskedasticity and OLS is still unbiased and consistent, but you need a robust standard error: the modern default for a cross-section.

Time series replace random sampling: strict exogeneity over all periods for the textbook result, or only the current period, stationarity and a HAC standard error once a lagged outcome enters. Panels add a unit effect: fixed effects lets it track the regressors; random effects assumes it does not, and buys precision. That is exactly the GLS page of today's talk.

直觉：同样八条假设，可以从强到弱打包成几个框架；每往下一层就放松一条。横截面默认用第 3 层加稳健标准误；时间序列看有没有滞后因变量；面板看个体效应会不会跟着解释变量走。

Textbook standard error
the usual OLS standard error of Wooldridge (2020), Introductory Econometrics, ch. 3 to 4 · the default in Stata reg, R lm and statsmodels

Var⁡^(b)=σ^2(X⊤X)−1\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(b)=\hat\sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}Var(b)=σ^2(X⊤X)−1: one noise level σ^2\hat\sigma^2σ^2 for every row.

Right only if every error is equally noisy and no two are correlated (A6, A7). If either fails, bbb is fine but this number is wrong.

HC1
heteroskedasticity-consistent, version 1: White (1980), times a small-sample factor · Wooldridge (2020), ch. 8 · Stata: vce(robust)

Lets every row have its own noise: the middle of the sandwich uses each row's squared residual, ∑ie^i2xixi⊤\sum_i \hat e_i^2 x_ix_i^\top∑i​e^i2​xi​xi⊤​, scaled by N/(N−K)N/(N-K)N/(N−K).

Still assumes the rows are independent. Our example: 0.0305 becomes 0.0369 (page 12).

HAC
heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent: Newey and West (1987) · Wooldridge (2020), ch. 12 · Stata: newey

For a time series: also lets nearby periods' errors move together. Products of residuals up to a chosen lag enter the middle of the sandwich, with weights that fade as the lag grows.

Assumes the correlation dies out with distance (weak dependence).

CR1
cluster-robust, version 1: Cameron and Miller (2015) · Stata: vce(cluster id)

First adds up each unit's terms, ∑txgte^gt\sum_t x_{gt}\hat e_{gt}∑t​xgt​e^gt​, then builds the sandwich from the GGG unit sums, scaled by GG−1N−1N−K\frac{G}{G-1}\frac{N-1}{N-K}G−1G​N−KN−1​. Any correlation inside a unit (a person, a firm) is allowed.

Assumes independent units, and many of them. Our example: 0.0369 becomes 0.0385 (page 12).

Cross-section

Default to 3 with a robust SE. Use 1 only with a small sample and believable normal errors.

Time series

No lagged outcome: 4a. With yt−1y_{t-1}yt−1​: 4b and a HAC SE. Non-stationary: neither; difference or cointegrate.

Panel

cgc_gcg​ may track XXX: FE. Unrelated by design (a conjoint): RE. Unsure: Hausman or Mundlak; reject, use FE.

The same five frameworks in one table, using today's labels A1 to A8. Black ticks are required, grey means not required, red means the assumption is replaced by a different version.

The arrows on top give the direction. One to three is a strict chain: each drops one assumption. Four and five are not looser than three; they adapt the list to time series and to panels. Inside each pair, 4b is looser than 4a, and random effects adds one assumption to fixed effects.

直觉：1 到 3 是一条严格放松的链；4 和 5 不是比 3 更宽松，而是换了数据结构。标准误那一行点开就能看到每种标准误假设了什么。

Central limit theorem: averaging erases the shape

The problem a test needs the sampling distribution of bbb, the OLS (ordinary least squares) estimate: how it would scatter over fresh samples. Yet b−β=(X⊤X)−1X⊤εb-\beta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\varepsilonb−β=(X⊤X)−1X⊤ε is an average of nnn pieces xiεix_i\varepsilon_ixi​εi​, and the shape of the error is unknown.

β\betaβ: the true coefficients; xix_ixi​: answer iii's regressors; εi=yi−xi⊤β\varepsilon_i=y_i-x_i^\top\betaεi​=yi​−xi⊤​β: its error. Here yiy_iyi​ is 0 or 1, so εi\varepsilon_iεi​ takes two values.

Two routes assume normal errors (A8): bbb is exactly normal, the ttt test exact at any nnn. Or let nnn grow and use the CLT (central limit theorem): approximately normal, no A8.

The theorem Z1,…,ZnZ_1,\dots,Z_nZ1​,…,Zn​ independent, one distribution, mean μ\muμ, finite variance σ2\sigma^2σ2:  n (Zˉ−μ)σ→dN(0,1)\ \dfrac{\sqrt n\,(\bar Z-\mu)}{\sigma}\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1) σn​(Zˉ−μ)​d​N(0,1)

Zˉ\bar ZZˉ: their average; →d\xrightarrow{d}d​: its distribution gets ever closer to N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1), the normal with mean 0 and variance 1.

Average few combinations reach the extremes, so averages pile up in the middle, and the spread shrinks: sd⁡(Zˉ)=σ/n\operatorname{sd}(\bar Z)=\sigma/\sqrt nsd(Zˉ)=σ/n​.

Right: Zi=yiZ_i=y_iZi​=yi​, one answer, with μ=0.735\mu=0.735μ=0.735 and σ=0.441\sigma=0.441σ=0.441.

Zoom by n\sqrt nn​ holding the width fixed, the shape that remains is the bell, whatever ZZZ was: only μ\muμ and σ\sigmaσ survive (D5 shows why).

Why can we run a t test without assuming normal errors? Start from the problem. To test, we need to know how b would scatter if we drew fresh samples: its sampling distribution. Written out, b minus the true beta is X transpose X inverse times X transpose epsilon: an average of n pieces, each a regressor times an error. And we do not know what the errors look like. Here y is 0 or 1, so each error takes only two values; nothing like a bell.

(Step.) There are two ways out. Assume the errors are normal, A8: then b is exactly normal and the t test is exact at any sample size. That is the classical linear model. Or let the sample grow and use the central limit theorem: b is then approximately normal, and A8 is not needed.

(Step.) The theorem: take independent draws from one distribution with mean mu and a finite variance sigma squared. Their average, centred and scaled by root n over sigma, has a distribution that gets ever closer to the standard normal. Nothing is said about the shape of each draw.

(Step.) Watch it on the right with one answer, accepted with probability 0.735. One answer is two spikes. Average two, five, thirty, six hundred: few combinations reach the extremes, so the averages pile up in the middle, and the spread shrinks like sigma over root n.

(Step.) Now zoom by root n, so the width stays fixed. The bars settle onto the bell: at n of 600 the largest gap between the two cumulative curves is 0.02. The two spikes are gone; only the mean and the spread survive. The next slide shows why only those two.

直觉：做 t 检验要知道 b 在重新抽样时怎么跳。b 是很多个误差的平均，而单个误差长什么样不知道（这里只取两个值）。要么假设误差是正态（A8），要么让样本变大：平均会把每个误差的形状抹掉，只留下均值和方差，所以放大 √n 倍之后看到的总是同一条钟形曲线。

Central limit theorem: why only the mean and the variance survive

What each moment of ZZZ leaves behind after the power nnn:

momentone factorafter nnn
mean, E[Z]=0E[Z]=0E[Z]=000
variance, E[Z2]=1E[Z^2]=1E[Z2]=1s2/(2n)s^2/(2n)s2/(2n)s2/2s^2/2s2/2, stays
skewness, E[Z3]E[Z^3]E[Z3]∝n−3/2\propto n^{-3/2}∝n−3/2∝n−1/2→0\propto n^{-1/2}\to0∝n−1/2→0
4th moment, E[Z4]E[Z^4]E[Z4]∝n−2\propto n^{-2}∝n−2∝n−1→0\propto n^{-1}\to0∝n−1→0

The two spikes of a yes or no answer are its skewness and higher moments: they fade like n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2. That is how fast the bell arrives (the Berry–Esseen theorem), so a skewed ZZZ needs a larger nnn.

Without an MMM that exists, use E[eisZ]E[e^{\mathrm{i}sZ}]E[eisZ] (with i=−1\mathrm{i}=\sqrt{-1}i=−1​), the characteristic function: the same algebra, for any ZZZ with finite variance.

Why the bell, and why only the mean and the variance? Standardise each draw so it has mean zero and variance one, and scale the sum by one over root n. We want to show its distribution tends to the standard normal.

(Step.) The tool is the moment generating function: the expected value of e to the s times the variable. Each distribution has its own, so if the functions match, the distributions match. s is just the argument. (Step.) Because the draws are independent, the expectation of the product splits into n factors, and because they share one distribution, the factors are equal: the function of the sum is the function of one draw, raised to the power n.

(Step.) Expand the function of one draw as a Taylor series. The coefficients are the moments: the mean, which is zero, the variance, which is one, then the skewness and so on. (Step.) Put v equal to s over root n. The variance term becomes s squared over 2n; the skewness term is of order n to the minus three halves.

(Step.) Raise to the power n. One plus a over n, to the power n, tends to e to the a: the variance term survives as s squared over two. The skewness term, added up n times, is still only of order one over root n, so it vanishes. (Step.) And e to the s squared over two is the moment generating function of the standard normal. The limit is normal whatever the draws looked like.

(Step.) The table on the right is the whole story: the mean contributes nothing, the variance stays, every higher moment fades. The two spikes of a yes or no answer live in those higher moments, and they fade like one over root n; the Berry–Esseen theorem turns that rate into a bound, so skewed data need a larger sample. When the moment generating function does not exist, the characteristic function does the same job for any variable with a finite variance.

直觉：矩母函数像分布的指纹。独立同分布的和，指纹就是单个指纹的 n 次方。把单个指纹按矩展开：均值是 0，方差那一项乘 n 次后留下来，偏度、峰度这些描述形状的项乘 n 次后仍然趋于 0。剩下的指纹只由方差决定，正好是正态分布的指纹。

Central limit theorem: from b to a t test and a p-value

OLS n (b−β)=(1nX⊤X)−1⏟→ Q−11n∑ixiεi⏟→ N(0, B)→dN(0, Q−1BQ−1)\sqrt n\,(b-\beta)=\underbrace{\bigl(\tfrac1nX^\top X\bigr)^{-1}}_{\to\,Q^{-1}}\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\textstyle\sum_i x_i\varepsilon_i}_{\to\,N(0,\,B)}\xrightarrow{d}N\bigl(0,\,Q^{-1}BQ^{-1}\bigr)n​(b−β)=→Q−1(n1​X⊤X)−1​​→N(0,B)n​1​∑i​xi​εi​​​d​N(0,Q−1BQ−1)

Only the variance is needed, and the residuals ei=yi−xi⊤be_i=y_i-x_i^\top bei​=yi​−xi⊤​b estimate it: B^=1n∑iei2xixi⊤\hat B=\tfrac1n\sum_i e_i^2x_ix_i^\topB^=n1​∑i​ei2​xi​xi⊤​. SE^\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}SE: the estimated standard error. Example: bk=0.06b_k=0.06bk​=0.06, SE^=0.0252\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}=0.0252SE=0.0252, so t=2.38t=2.38t=2.38.

Area is probability  Φ(z)=∫−∞zϕ(u) du,  ϕ(u)=12πe−u2/2\ \Phi(z)=\int_{-\infty}^{z}\phi(u)\,du,\ \ \phi(u)=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-u^2/2} Φ(z)=∫−∞z​ϕ(u)du,  ϕ(u)=2π​1​e−u2/2

ϕ\phiϕ: the bell's height (a density, not a probability); Φ(z)\Phi(z)Φ(z): the area left of zzz, which the normal table lists. Φ(2.38)=0.9913\Phi(2.38)=0.9913Φ(2.38)=0.9913, so p=2 [1−Φ(∣t∣)]=0.017p=2\,[1-\Phi(|t|)]=0.017p=2[1−Φ(∣t∣)]=0.017.

The threshold Φ(1.96)=0.975\Phi(1.96)=0.975Φ(1.96)=0.975 leaves 2.5% in each tail: ∣t∣>1.96|t|>1.96∣t∣>1.96 exactly when p<0.05p<0.05p<0.05.

What it replaces A8 (normality). A6 and A7 move to HC1 and CR1, a CLT over people, so it needs many. Still needed: A3, independent draws with finite variance. It cannot fix bias: without the coin the bell is just as neat, around 0.55.

Back to OLS. Root n times b minus beta is a product of two pieces. The first, the inverse of X transpose X over n, settles down to a fixed matrix Q by the law of large numbers. The second, the sum of x times epsilon over root n, is exactly what the central limit theorem is about: its mean is zero under A5, and its variance is B, the expected squared error times x x transpose. Put together, b is approximately normal with the sandwich variance, Q inverse B Q inverse, the sandwich of D29. With equal variances, A6, B is sigma squared Q and we are back to the textbook formula.

(Step.) The theorem needs only the variance, and the variance can be estimated from what we see, the residuals. That answers the worry that the errors are unobservable: we never need their shape. So the t statistic, the estimate over its estimated standard error, is approximately standard normal when the true coefficient is zero. Example: an estimate of 0.06 with a standard error of 0.0252 gives t equal to 2.38.

(Step.) How likely is a t that far from zero? Probability is area under the bell. The height of the bell, phi, is a density, not a probability; the area to the left of z is capital Phi, and that is what the normal table lists. Watch the shaded area grow on the right while the lower curve rises: the lower curve's height at 2.38 is 0.9913. One tail is 0.0087, both tails 0.017: that is the p-value.

(Step.) Where does 1.96 come from? Capital Phi of 1.96 is 0.975, leaving 2.5 percent in each tail, 5 percent in all. So a t beyond 1.96 and a p below 0.05 are the same statement.

(Step.) What the theorem buys: it replaces A8. A6 and A7 are handled by robust and clustered standard errors; the clustered version is a central limit theorem over people, so it needs many of them. It still needs independent draws with a finite variance. And it cannot fix bias: without the coin the readings form an equally neat bell, centred on 0.55, as on page 4.

直觉：b 是 X 的部分（大数定律收敛到 Q）乘上误差的平均（中心极限定理给出正态），所以 b 近似正态，方差就是三明治。方差能用残差估计，所以不需要知道误差长什么样。概率是钟形曲线下的面积：Φ(z) 是 z 左边的面积，查表就是读它；两边尾巴加起来就是 p 值，1.96 正好在两边各留 2.5%。CLT 替代了 A8，但纠正不了偏误。

The AMCE compares potential answers

Every row iii (respondent ggg, task ttt) has four potential answers (potential outcomes) Yi(s,r)Y_i(s,r)Yi​(s,r), one per possible offer. We see only one.

yi=Yi(Si,Ri)y_i=Y_i(S_i,R_i)yi​=Yi​(Si​,Ri​)
consistency: what we record is the potential answer to the offer actually shown
τS≡E[Yi(1,Ri)−Yi(0,Ri)]\tau_S\equiv E\left[Y_i(1,R_i)-Y_i(0,R_i)\right]τS​≡E[Yi​(1,Ri​)−Yi​(0,Ri​)]

Keep the remote level the design drew, switch salary from low to high, average the change.

τS=Pr⁡(Ri=1) Δ1+Pr⁡(Ri=0) Δ0\tau_S=\hl{\Pr(R_i=1)}\,\Delta_1+\hl{\Pr(R_i=0)}\,\Delta_0τS​=Pr(Ri​=1)Δ1​+Pr(Ri​=0)Δ0​

Condition on RiR_iRi​, which the design draws independently of the potential answers; Δr≡E[Yi(1,r)−Yi(0,r)]\Delta_r\equiv E\left[Y_i(1,r)-Y_i(0,r)\right]Δr​≡E[Yi​(1,r)−Yi​(0,r)] is the salary effect at remote level rrr.

The design sets the weights. Ours: τS=12(0.33)+12(0.33)=0.33\tau_S=\tfrac12(0.33)+\tfrac12(0.33)=0.33τS​=21​(0.33)+21​(0.33)=0.33.

Three assumptions make τS\tau_SτS​ recoverable from data (Hainmueller, Hopkins & Yamamoto 2014).

AssumptionSaysBuys
C1 stability, no carryoverthe answer depends only on the offer shown now, the same way in every taskYi(s,r)Y_i(s,r)Yi​(s,r) is well defined; one person's six tasks can be pooled
C2 no profile-order effectswhere a profile sits on the screen does not matterpositions can be pooled (trivial here: one offer per task)
C3 randomisation(Si,Ri)⊥{Yi(s,r)}(S_i,R_i)\perp\{Y_i(s,r)\}(Si​,Ri​)⊥{Yi​(s,r)}, and every profile can occuridentification: a difference in means recovers τS\tau_SτS​

C3 is the only one the researcher controls completely: the random number generator guarantees it, not anybody's beliefs about respondents.

Before any estimator, we need the number we are after. For every row, imagine the four answers that person would have given to the four possible offers: the potential answers. We see only one; this row was shown the high-salary office offer and accepted it. Consistency links the two: we record the potential answer to the offer actually shown.

The AMCE keeps each row's remote level as the design drew it, switches salary from low to high, and averages the change. Conditioning on remote shows that it is a weighted average of the salary effect for remote and for office jobs, with the design setting the red weights. Both effects are 0.33 here, so the AMCE is 0.33. The proof on the next slide turns on those weights, and two slides on we change them on purpose.

Three assumptions make it recoverable (Hainmueller, Hopkins and Yamamoto): no carryover, no effect of screen position, and randomisation, the only one the researcher fully controls.

直觉：每个回答背后都有四个“如果当时看到的是那份 offer 会怎么答”，我们只看得到其中一个。AMCE 就是把薪资从低换成高，平均下来接受的概率变了多少。

Because we shuffled, comparing averages is enough

Rewrite the acceptance rate of high-salary offers until only potential answers are left.

The proof never used a regression, linearity, normality, or independence of one person's six answers. The design did the work.

So the gap of 0.55 mixes in part of the remote effect; the OLS section measures how much.

Fix: compare within remote levels, weight each by one half:

Now the proof that the shuffle is enough. Take the acceptance rate among high-salary offers. Consistency turns it into potential answers; on this event salary is high; iterated expectations split by remote level.

The red step is where randomisation enters: profiles were drawn independently of the potential answers, and salary independently of remote, so the weights are the plain shares of remote work. Do the same for low salary and subtract: you get the definition from the previous slide. No regression, no linearity, no normality was used.

Randomised, that is 0.735 minus 0.405, 0.33. Observational, the weights break: five in six high-salary offers are remote but only one in six low-salary offers, so the gap of 0.55 carries part of the remote effect; the OLS section measures how much. Comparing within remote levels restores 0.33, but only if salary is as good as random within each level, which no data can check. OLS on salary returns these same gaps: it is the calculator, not the reason.

直觉：是电脑抽签决定哪份 offer 拿高薪，所以高薪组和低薪组在别的方面平均一样，两组接受率之差只能来自薪资。回归只是算这个差的工具，识别靠的是设计。

The AMCE depends on how often the other attribute appears

Let π≡Pr⁡(Ri=1)\pi\equiv\Pr(R_i=1)π≡Pr(Ri​=1) be the share of remote profiles in the design. The expanded definition is a line in π\piπ:

τS(π)=π Δ1+(1−π) Δ0\tau_S(\pi)=\pi\,\Delta_1+(1-\pi)\,\Delta_0τS​(π)=πΔ1​+(1−π)Δ0​

Its slope is Δ1−Δ0\nv{\Delta_1-\Delta_0}Δ1​−Δ0​. The AMCE is the same for every design exactly when Δ1=Δ0\Delta_1=\Delta_0Δ1​=Δ0​: the salary effect is the same for remote and office jobs (no interaction on the probability scale).
