de la Cuesta, Egami & Imai (2022): choose π\piπ to match a target population (the real share of remote jobs), by design or by reweighting. Either way, report π\piπ next to every AMCE (Hainmueller et al. 2014).

The weights in the definition are a choice. Write pi for the share of remote profiles in the design. The AMCE is then a straight line in pi, with slope Delta one minus Delta zero.

In our additive data the line is flat at 0.33, so this critique never shows in our numbers; that is a property of the example, not of conjoint experiments. Toggle to world H, which is invented: salary matters little for remote jobs, 0.10, and a lot for office jobs, 0.50. Drag pi: 0.42 at 0.2, 0.30 at one half, 0.18 at 0.8. Same people, three different effects of salary, set only by how often the researcher showed remote offers.

De la Cuesta, Egami and Imai recommend matching the attribute distribution to a target population, by design or by reweighting. Hainmueller, Hopkins and Yamamoto already asked that the weighting distribution always be reported with the AMCE. They suggested the uniform distribution as a default; de la Cuesta and coauthors argue it is a choice, not a neutral default.

直觉：AMCE 是按实验里各种 offer 出现的比例加权平均出来的。只要两个属性有交互作用，比例一变，AMCE 就跟着变；均匀随机也是一种选择，不是中立的默认值。

An AMCE is not a vote, and subgroups need marginal means

Same AMCE, very different shares of answers that favour high salary (Abramson, Koçak & Magazinnik 2022). Say “high salary raises the average acceptance probability by 0.33”, never “most respondents prefer a high salary”.

MM (marginal mean): the acceptance rate of one level, averaged over the design's mix of the other attribute:

MM(s)≡E[Yi(s,Ri)]\mathrm{MM}(s)\equiv E[Y_i(s,R_i)]MM(s)≡E[Yi​(s,Ri​)]

Ours: MM(1)=12(0.90)+12(0.57)=0.735\mathrm{MM}(1)=\tfrac12(0.90)+\tfrac12(0.57)=0.735MM(1)=21​(0.90)+21​(0.57)=0.735 and MM(0)=0.405\mathrm{MM}(0)=0.405MM(0)=0.405. Their difference is the AMCE, 0.33.

Between subgroups AAA and BBB, a gap in AMCEs also carries the reference level:

τSA−τSB=[MMA(1)−MMB(1)]−[MMA(0)−MMB(0)]\begin{aligned}\tau_S^{A}-\tau_S^{B}&=\bigl[\mathrm{MM}^{A}(1)-\mathrm{MM}^{B}(1)\bigr]\\&\quad-\hl{\bigl[\mathrm{MM}^{A}(0)-\mathrm{MM}^{B}(0)\bigr]}\end{aligned}τSA​−τSB​​=[MMA(1)−MMB(1)]−[MMA(0)−MMB(0)]​
Hypothetical salary levellowmediumhigh
MM in subgroup A0.300.600.80

High vs low: A 0.50, B 0.40. High vs medium: A 0.20, B 0.30. The sign of the gap flips, yet both accept high-salary offers at 0.80 (Leeper, Hobolt & Tilley 2020).

Two more things the AMCE does not say. First, it is not a vote. For one answer the salary effect is plus one, zero or minus one, so the AMCE is the share flipping towards accepting minus the share flipping against. Thirty-three percent flipping one way gives 0.33; so does 66.5 percent one way and 33.5 the other. Both populations are hypothetical. So say "high salary raises the average acceptance probability by 0.33", never "most respondents prefer a high salary" (Abramson, Koçak and Magazinnik).

Second, subgroups. A marginal mean is the acceptance rate of one level, averaged over the design's mix: 0.735 for high salary, 0.405 for low. A gap between two subgroups' AMCEs also contains how they treat the reference level, the red bracket. In the hypothetical table, A looks keener with low as the reference, B with medium, yet both accept high-salary offers at 0.80. Leeper, Hobolt and Tilley: report marginal means.

直觉：AMCE 是净差额，不是投票的票数；比较两个人群时，先看每个水平各自的边际均值，别直接拿两个 AMCE 相减。

In the population, with SSS binary, independent of RRR, and (S,R)(S,R)(S,R) independent of the potential answers, the additive regression's coefficient βS∗\beta^*_SβS∗​ (the limit of bSb_SbS​) is

the AMCE, even if the truth has an S×RS\times RS×R interaction.

Start with the simplest regression: a constant and one dummy. A dummy squared is itself, so X transpose X holds just the counts. Its determinant is N one times N zero, so the inverse exists exactly when both groups have a row: A2 in its most concrete form. Multiply through: the intercept is the low-salary rate and the slope is the difference in rates, 0.33 in one design and 0.55 in the other. What makes 0.33 causal is the shuffle, not the regression.

Now add remote. Frisch-Waugh-Lovell: take out of salary whatever remote predicts, and regress y on the rest. Randomised, remote predicts nothing, the residual is S minus one half, and the regression with remote equals the one without it, by algebra.

The population version is why a conjoint can use the additive regression: with salary binary and assigned independently of remote and of the potential answers, the coefficient is the AMCE even if the truth has an interaction (section 4.3 of the notes).

直觉：只有一个虚拟变量时，回归什么也没多做，它就是两组接受率相减；这个差值算不算因果效应，取决于设计（随机洗牌），而不是回归。加入远程之后，FWL（Frisch-Waugh-Lovell 定理）告诉我们系数只看“远程预测不了的那部分薪水”；随机设计里远程什么也预测不了，所以长短回归一模一样。

Controlling for remote rescues 0.33 here only because, within each remote group, salary was assigned as if at random. In real data that is an assumption, not a fact.

Call the regression on salary alone the short one and the one with remote the long one. Because the long regression's residuals are orthogonal to every regressor, the two are tied by an exact identity: short equals long plus delta times the remote coefficient, where delta is the slope from regressing remote on salary.

Start the slider at 50 percent, the randomised design: delta is zero and both numbers sit on 0.33. Drag to 83 percent, our observational design: delta is two thirds, and the short regression drifts to 0.55, which is 0.33 plus two thirds of 0.33. The long one stays put, but only because within each remote group salary was assigned as if at random. In real data that is an assumption, not a fact.

The 200 surprising offers carry 5/6 of the weight and sit at p=0.57p=0.57p=0.57, the noisiest cells. The SE (standard error) grows by the square root of the ratio of the two averages:

0.0305×√(0.2270/0.1544)=0.0305×1.21=0.03690.0305\times\surd(0.2270/0.1544)=0.0305\times1.21=\hl{0.0369}0.0305×√(0.2270/0.1544)=0.0305×1.21=0.0369

Randomised: S~i=±0.5\tilde S_i=\pm0.5S~i​=±0.5 in every row, so the weights are the row shares, the two averages coincide, and textbook === HC1 =0.0252=0.0252=0.0252.

A yes or no answer has a variance we can write down: p times one minus p. The rate differs across cells, so the error variance does too, 0.09 in the best cell and 0.245 in the two middle cells. A6 fails by construction.

Drop A6, keep A5 and A7, and the variance of b becomes a sandwich with a diagonal Omega in the middle. White's trick: we never need 1,200 separate variances, only the three-by-three sum in the middle, and squared residuals get that sum right in large samples. HC1 (heteroskedasticity-consistent, version 1) adds N over N minus K; it is what Stata calls robust.

For salary, FWL turns this into one ratio: the row variances averaged with weights proportional to S-tilde squared. In the observational table the two small off-diagonal cells take five sixths of the weight, and they are the noisiest cells, at 0.57. Weighted average 0.2270 against a plain 0.1544: the SE (standard error) grows by the square root of the ratio, 1.21, from 0.0305 to 0.0369.

Randomised, every S-tilde is plus or minus one half, the weights are equal, and robust equals textbook to the last digit.

直觉：二元结果的方差是 p(1−p)，越接近一半越难预测。观察设计里决定薪水系数的，恰好是那 200 个“高薪却坐班、低薪却远程”的 offer，而它们正落在最嘈杂的 0.57 格子里，所以稳健标准误变大。

One person, six answers: the errors come in blocks

Answer ttt of respondent ggg: εgt=cg+ugt\varepsilon_{gt}=c_g+u_{gt}εgt​=cg​+ugt​. The personal tendency cgc_gcg​ sits in all TTT answers, so errors correlate inside a person and not across people. A7 fails only inside the blocks.

CR (cluster-robust): for each person first add up Xg⊤egX_g^\top e_gXg⊤​eg​ (regressors times residuals over their six answers), then treat the 200 sums as independent.

V^CR=(X⊤X)−1(∑gXg⊤egeg⊤Xg)(X⊤X)−1\widehat V_{\mathrm{CR}}=(X^\top X)^{-1}\left(\sum_g X_g^\top e_ge_g^\top X_g\right)(X^\top X)^{-1}VCR​=(X⊤X)−1(∑g​Xg⊤​eg​eg⊤​Xg​)(X⊤X)−1

Needs many independent clusters, not a model of the block.

How far should the SE move? Equal blocks (Moulton 1990; this product form: Cameron & Miller 2015):

true variance of bStextbook variance=1+(T−1) ρx~ ρε\frac{\text{true variance of }b_S}{\text{textbook variance}}=1+(T-1)\,\nv{\rho_{\tilde x}}\,\rho_\varepsilontextbook variancetrue variance of bS​​=1+(T−1)ρx~​ρε​

ρx~\rho_{\tilde x}ρx~​: how alike one person's values of the regressor (S~\tilde SS~ here) are. Our shuffled salary: ρx~=−0.016\rho_{\tilde x}=-0.016ρx~​=−0.016; with the residual correlation ρe=0.24\rho_e=0.24ρe​=0.24 for ρε\rho_\varepsilonρε​, the factor is 0.98. A trait fixed within person, ρx~=1\rho_{\tilde x}=1ρx~​=1, gives 2.20: the SE is 1.48 times larger.

(Figure, from the third step.) The strip under each person shows each answer's regressor, filled above its mean, hollow below. Our salary measured a within-person correlation of the regressor of minus 0.016, which is chance; the toggle uses 0.

Someone who likes offers in general says yes more often in all six answers. So write the error as a personal part c-g plus an answer-specific part u: errors correlate inside a person, not across people. Blocks on the diagonal, zeros outside.

The cluster-robust estimator keeps the OLS estimate and changes only the meat: add up regressors times residuals over each person's six answers, then treat those 200 sums as independent. It needs many clusters, not a model of the block. With one row per cluster it is White's estimator from the previous slide.

Will it matter? Only if the regressor is also alike within a person. Moulton showed the extreme case, a regressor constant within each group, where the factor is one plus (T minus one) times rho; Cameron and Miller write the general product form on the slide. Salary was shuffled within person, so same-person pairs push the variance up and down about equally; the factor stays near one however far you drag rho, 0.98 with our measured minus 0.016. Switch to a respondent-level regressor such as an age band: the blocks turn solid, and at T six and rho 0.24 the variance is 2.20 times the textbook one, the SE 1.48 times.

直觉：同一个人的六个答案误差相关，但标准误要不要放大，还要看解释变量在同一个人内部是不是也“抱团”。薪水在每个人内部被洗过牌，个人口味正负抵消；换成每个人固定不变的变量，标准误就要放大约 1.5 倍。

So far, whenever A6 and A7 failed we kept OLS and repaired its standard errors. GLS asks: if I write down the shape of the error covariance, can I get a better estimator, not just honest standard errors?

Aitken's trick: find P with P transpose P equal to Omega inverse, by diagonalising Omega. Multiply the whole model by P. The coefficients do not change, but the errors become spherical again, so Gauss-Markov applies to the transformed data and OLS on them, the boxed formula, is BLUE (best linear unbiased estimator). Since anything linear in y is also linear in P y, ordinary OLS is one of the competitors it beats.

On the right, the first-order condition is our one equation with the weight Omega inverse. With unequal variances only, the weight is one over each row's variance: noisy rows count less. With one block per respondent it is a six by six matrix: a residual is judged together with the same person's other five answers.

Random effects is GLS with one particular Omega: every answer carries the person's tendency c, so any two answers of one person share the variance sigma c squared.

Slow down for line two. Split each person's six answers into their mean and the deviations from it. Omega scales the deviations by sigma u squared and the mean by sigma u squared plus T sigma c squared, so the inverse square root works coefficient by coefficient: the identity minus theta times the averaging matrix, with theta from the box. Rho is the intraclass correlation, about 0.24 here, as on the clustering slide.

So: from each answer and every regressor, subtract theta times the person's mean. Theta zero is pooled OLS, theta one is fixed effects. Move the sliders: theta rises with rho and with T. Ours: T six, rho 0.2427, theta 0.4151, from variances estimated on pooled OLS residuals, which is feasible GLS. GLS buys efficiency by believing more

Why not exactly 0.33? GLS mixes two contrasts, within persons (0.3201) and between persons (0.3499), and gives the between one weight (1−θ^)2=0.3421(1-\hat\theta)^2=0.3421(1−θ^)2=0.3421 instead of 1; the weights are matrices, so a little of the remote contrast leaks in too. What it must believe: E(cg∣Xg)=0\hl{E(c_g\mid X_g)=0}E(cg​∣Xg​)=0, a person's tendency to accept is unrelated to the offers they saw.

In a conjoint the random device deals every profile without looking at the respondent: guaranteed by design. With real offers to real job seekers it is strong: the more employable may get more high-salary offers and accept more.

Mundlak (1978): add each person's average attributes zˉg\bar z_gzˉg​ as regressors; random effects then returns the fixed-effects slope exactly (balanced panel), and testing their coefficients asks the data about E(cg∣Xg)=0E(c_g\mid X_g)=0E(cg​∣Xg​)=0 (a test can raise an alarm, not certify).

Same data, two numbers. Pooled OLS: 0.3300, cluster-robust SE 0.0240. Random-effects GLS: 0.3241, model-based SE 0.0232, and its cluster-robust SE is also 0.0232, so the comparison is like for like. Slightly more precise, as GLS theory promises when the variance model is right.

Why not exactly 0.33? Each estimate mixes a within-person contrast, 0.3201, and a between-person contrast, 0.3499. OLS uses both at full weight; GLS turns the between part down to 0.3421 of its weight. The gap is a quarter of a standard error: noise, not bias.

The price is the red assumption: a person's tendency to accept must be unrelated to the offers they saw. A conjoint guarantees it. In an observational panel it is a real bet; if it fails GLS is inconsistent, and only fixed effects survives. Choosing between them there changes the identifying assumption, not the decimals.

Model-based SEs need the right Omega: in the observational design 0.0288 against a cluster-robust 0.0351. So report GLS with cluster SEs, and use Mundlak's regression to let the data raise an alarm.

直觉：GLS 多相信一点“误差长什么样”，换来更小的标准误；代价是要相信每个人的性格和他看到的 offer 无关。随机化的 conjoint 白送这个假设，观察数据里就得自己掏钱。

The one equation again, with wi=1w_i=1wi​=1 and μi=Λ(xi⊤β)\mu_i=\Lambda(x_i^\top\beta)μi​=Λ(xi⊤​β).

The weight is 1 because the slope Λ′\Lambda'Λ′ equals the Bernoulli variance pi(1−pi)p_i(1-p_i)pi​(1−pi​), and the two cancel. Differentiate once more:

H(β)=−∑ipi(1−pi) xixi⊤H(\beta)=-\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)\,x_ix_i^\topH(β)=−i∑​pi​(1−pi​)xi​xi⊤​

No yyy in it, and negative definite under A2: log⁡L\log LlogL is strictly concave, so a root of the score is the unique maximum. Newton steps find it.

If the logit shape is right, the MLE (maximum likelihood estimator) is consistent and asymptotically efficient (under regularity conditions), not unbiased: a separated sample (say, every high-salary offer accepted) has no finite β^\hat\betaβ^​, so E[β^]E[\hat\beta]E[β^​] is not even defined. If the shape is wrong, it is consistent only for the best logit approximation.

GLS kept the straight line and changed the weights; logit keeps the weights and changes the shape. It keeps the linear index but passes it through the S-shaped logistic curve, so every prediction is a probability. The latent utility is one way to motivate it; nothing below needs that story.

Line one: each answer is a Bernoulli draw, so the log-likelihood is a sum. Line two is the one calculus fact we need: the slope of the logistic curve is Lambda times one minus Lambda. Line three: the score is the gradient of log L, not log L itself. The p times one minus p from the chain rule cancels the denominators, and the boxed line is left: the OLS normal equations with the fitted probability where x transpose b used to be.

On the right: the Hessian has no y in it and is negative definite under full rank, so the log-likelihood is a single hill. Mind the wording: the MLE (maximum likelihood estimator) is consistent and asymptotically efficient when the logit is the right model; it is not unbiased, and where the shape is wrong, as here, it converges to a pseudo-true value.

直觉：logit 只是把直线换成 S 形曲线，记账规则不变：每一行的残差乘上自己的回归元，加起来等于零；权重刚好是 1，因为 logistic 曲线的斜率正好等于伯努利方差。

The log-likelihood has one peak, and the score is zero there

How sharp the peak is gives the standard error, if the shape is right.

Right shape (true value β∘\beta^\circβ∘): the information matrix equality I=E[ss⊤]\mathcal I=E[ss^\top]I=E[ss⊤] holds, and β^logit∼aN(β∘, I(β∘)−1)\hat\beta_{\mathrm{logit}}\overset{a}{\sim}N\bigl(\beta^\circ,\ \mathcal I(\beta^\circ)^{-1}\bigr)β^​logit​∼aN(β∘, I(β∘)−1).

This is the logit log-likelihood of our randomised data, computed in the browser from the four cell counts, 270, 171, 171 and 72 acceptances out of 300, with the intercept held at its MLE so that we can draw the other two coefficients. Drag it: one smooth hill. The red point is the top, 1.6291 for both coefficients, where the score is zero.

How sharp the top is measures information, and its inverse gives the model-based SE, 0.1385. (The slice alone looks sharper, about 0.10, because it holds the intercept fixed; computed in Python from the four cell counts with the glm function of job_offer_example.py.) That number needs the logit shape to be right. Ours is not, as the next slide shows, so we use the sandwich with scores summed within respondent: 0.1336. Clustering barely moves it, because the attributes were shuffled independently of who answered. The odds-ratio interval is 3.9247 to 6.6259 around 5.0995: asymmetric, as every ratio interval is.

直觉：极大似然就是爬山，score 是坡度，山顶处坡度为零；山顶越尖，数据给的信息越多。形状设错了，山顶还在，但“尖度”不再等于真实的不确定性，所以用三明治。

The factor G over G minus one in front is a small-sample convention, not part of Liang and Zeger: Cameron and Miller (2015) note that Stata uses it for nonlinear models.

An odds ratio reads differently at every baseline

The logit is additive in the log-odds, so high salary multiplies the odds p/(1−p)p/(1-p)p/(1−p) by eβSe^{\beta_S}eβS​ whatever the baseline:

log⁡p1−p=β0+βSS+βRR\log\frac{p}{1-p}=\beta_0+\beta_S S+\beta_R Rlog1−pp​=β0​+βS​S+βR​R

On the probability scale the same odds ratio moves a baseline p0=Λ(z0)p_0=\Lambda(z_0)p0​=Λ(z0​) by Λ(z0+βS)−Λ(z0)\Lambda(z_0+\beta_S)-\Lambda(z_0)Λ(z0​+βS​)−Λ(z0​): largest when the step straddles 0.5 (from a baseline of 0.31 when βS=1.6291\beta_S=1.6291βS​=1.6291), never more than βS/4\beta_S/4βS​/4.

salary effectprobabilitylog-oddsodds ratio
office, 0.24 to 0.57+0.331.43454.20
remote, 0.57 to 0.90+0.331.91546.79
additive logit (office, remote)0.3699, 0.29011.62915.0995

Our truth is additive in probability, so no single βS\beta_SβS​ fits both strata: the additive logit is misspecified here. Its 1.6291 is a design-weighted compromise, closer to the office step, and not the simple average 1.6750.

The logit is a straight line in the log-odds, so e to the beta multiplies the odds by the same factor at every baseline. Odds are not probabilities: the probability does not become five times larger.

Use the sliders. With the logit's odds ratio, 5.10, its own office baseline 0.22 goes to 0.59, a gain of 0.37; a baseline of 0.90 goes only to 0.98. The gain is largest when the move straddles one half, 0.31 to 0.69, and never more than beta over four, 0.41 (computed in Python from the logistic formula with 1.6291).

Now the navy points, our data. High salary moves acceptance from 0.24 to 0.57 for office jobs and from 0.57 to 0.90 for remote ones: the same 0.33. In log-odds those are 1.4345 and 1.9154, because the second step climbs the flat top of the S. One coefficient cannot be both, so the additive logit is misspecified, and its 1.6291 is a compromise set by the design, closer to the office step. The observational design gives 1.6534 from the same truth.

直觉：同一个优势比，放在不同的起点上，换算成概率差大小完全不同。我们的真实效应在概率上等距，在对数优势上就不等距，所以 logit 只能交出一个由设计决定的折中值。

Odds ratios do not average, risk differences do

With no confounding, the pooled control and treated risks average the stratum risks with the same weights q(r)q(r)q(r), the stratum shares. A difference of two such averages is the average of the differences, so the RD (risk difference) collapses:

RDpooled=∑rq(r) RD(r)\mathrm{RD}_{\text{pooled}}=\sum_r q(r)\,\mathrm{RD}(r)RDpooled​=∑r​q(r)RD(r)

Here 0.2786=12(0.30+0.2571)0.2786=\tfrac12(0.30+0.2571)0.2786=21​(0.30+0.2571).

Odds bend the average: the odds of an average risk are not the average of the odds, so the odds ratio has no such identity. The pooled 3.1667 sits below both stratum values, which no weighted average can do.

Gail, Wieand & Piantadosi (1984): in a randomised experiment, leaving out a balanced covariate that predicts the outcome pulls the logit coefficient towards zero; linear and log-link coefficients do not move. Our data: OR (odds ratio) 5.0995 with remote, 4.0748 without. Two different estimands, neither biased.

This example is not from the job data. Two equal strata with baselines 0.2 and 0.6, the same odds ratio 4 in both, and treatment independent of stratum: no confounding at all. Pool them and the odds ratio is 3.1667, below 4 in both strata. Drag the slider: for any common odds ratio above one, the pooled one stays below it.

Risk differences behave: the pooled risks average the stratum risks with the same weights, so the pooled difference is the average of the differences, 0.2786 from 0.30 and 0.2571. Odds bend the risk, so the odds ratio has no such identity, and no average can sit below both of its inputs.

Gail, Wieand and Piantadosi: in a randomised experiment, dropping a balanced covariate that predicts the outcome moves the logit coefficient towards zero, while linear and log-link coefficients stay. Ours: 5.0995 with remote, 4.0748 without. A conditional and a marginal odds ratio: two estimands, neither biased.

直觉：风险差是线性的，先平均再相减等于先相减再平均；优势比要先过一道弯的换算，所以不能平均。控制变量一换，优势比就跟着变，这不叫偏误，是换了一个问题在问。

Under exact balance the logit average marginal effect is the difference in means

The AME (average marginal effect) switches salary on and off in every row and averages the change in the fitted probability: AME^S=1N∑i[p^(1,Ri)−p^(0,Ri)]\widehat{\mathrm{AME}}_S=\frac1N\sum_i\left[\hat p(1,R_i)-\hat p(0,R_i)\right]AMES​=N1​∑i​[p^​(1,Ri​)−p^​(0,Ri​)].

Theorem. Logit with an intercept and SSS, other regressors functions of RRR, a finite MLE, and RRR exactly balanced across SSS: then AME^S=yˉ1−yˉ0\widehat{\mathrm{AME}}_S=\bar y_1-\bar y_0AMES​=yˉ​1​−yˉ​0​, whatever the true shape.

group rows by RRR; qs(r)q_s(r)qs​(r): share of the S=sS=sS=s rows with R=rR=rR=r
AME^S=∑rq(r)[p^(1,r)−p^(0,r)]=yˉ1−yˉ0\widehat{\mathrm{AME}}_S=\sum_r q(r)\bigl[\hat p(1,r)-\hat p(0,r)\bigr]=\bar y_1-\bar y_0AMES​=∑r​q(r)[p^​(1,r)−p^​(0,r)]=yˉ​1​−yˉ​0​
group the AME the same way, q(r)q(r)q(r): share in the whole sample; balance, q1(r)=q0(r)=q(r)q_1(r)=q_0(r)=q(r)q1​(r)=q0​(r)=q(r), and line 2 give the last step

Here AME^S=0.7350−0.4050=0.3300\widehat{\mathrm{AME}}_S=0.7350-0.4050=\hl{0.3300}AMES​=0.7350−0.4050=0.3300, although our logit is misspecified. The proof never uses the values of β^\hat\betaβ^​.

Without exact balance it is only approximate; in observational data the shape matters (cells 500/100/200/400: logit AME 0.3356, not 0.33).

Now the good news. The average marginal effect switches salary on and off in every row and averages the change in the fitted probability. Under exact balance it equals the difference in means, 0.3300, even though our logit is misspecified.

Three lines. One: the score equations for the intercept and for salary say the fitted probabilities average to the observed rate within each salary group. Two: group those rows by remote, so each observed rate is a weighted average of fitted cells. Three: the AME (average marginal effect) uses the same fitted cells with whole-sample shares; balance makes the shares equal, so the AME is the difference of the observed means. The coefficients never enter.

It needs exact balance. Without it the result is approximate, and in observational data the shape matters: with 500, 100, 200 and 400 rows the logit AME is 0.3356, although the effect is 0.33 in every stratum. Our own observational design also gives 0.3300, but only because it is symmetric.

直觉：平衡设计下，logit 的 AME 被截距和 salary 的两条 score 方程钉死，形状设错也照样等于均值差；一旦不平衡，形状就成了识别假设的一部分。

Poisson's score only needs the mean to be right

PPML (Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood) sets μi=exp⁡(xi⊤β)\mu_i=\exp(x_i^\top\beta)μi​=exp(xi⊤​β), so eβSe^{\beta_S}eβS​ multiplies the acceptance rate. Pretend, for one slide, that yi∣xiy_i\mid x_iyi​∣xi​ is Poisson.

This holds whatever the variance, the share of zeros, or whether yyy is a count (Gourieroux, Monfort & Trognon 1984). One way only: a wrong mean still has a root, so β^\hat\betaβ^​ goes to a pseudo-true β∗\beta^*β∗ (as with the logit) and nothing flags the error.

The likelihood is scaffolding: what PPML solves is a set of moment conditions, E[x (y−μ)]=0E[x\,(y-\mu)]=0E[x(y−μ)]=0.

PPML, Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood, is the estimator for effects stated as ratios: e to the salary coefficient multiplies the acceptance rate. Pretend for one slide that the outcome is a Poisson count; line one is its log-likelihood.

Line two: the score, the gradient of log L, is a sum of x times y minus mu: the one equation again, with an exponential mean and weight one. The Hessian has no y and is negative definite under full rank, so a root is the unique maximum.

Line three is the key. Take the expectation of one row's score at the true value, conditioning on x first: y enters only through its mean, so the bracket is zero as soon as the mean is exponential. Variance, zeros, integers: none of it enters (Gourieroux, Monfort and Trognon). But only one way round: a wrong mean still has a root, a pseudo-true value, and nothing flags the error.

The table is the full list. Identification is the population version of A2, not strict concavity, which only makes the computed number unique. Inference also needs a finite meat B.

直觉：方程里 y 只以“y 减均值”出现，先在每个 x 上取平均，就只剩“均值公式对不对”这一件事；Poisson 似然只是搭架子，真正承重的是矩条件。

log-OLS answers a different question when E[log⁡η∣x]E[\log\eta\mid x]E[logη∣x] moves with xxx

Multiplicative model: y=exp⁡(x⊤β) ηy=\exp(x^\top\beta)\,\etay=exp(x⊤β)η with E[η∣x]=1E[\eta\mid x]=1E[η∣x]=1, so the target is log⁡E[y∣x]=x⊤β\log E[y\mid x]=x^\top\betalogE[y∣x]=x⊤β. Log first, then average:

E[log⁡y∣x]=x⊤β+E[log⁡η∣x]E[\log y\mid x]=x^\top\beta+\hl{E[\log\eta\mid x]}E[logy∣x]=x⊤β+E[logη∣x]

log-OLS consistently estimates the slope of E[log⁡y∣x]E[\log y\mid x]E[logy∣x]. It equals the slope we want, that of log⁡E[y∣x]\log E[y\mid x]logE[y∣x], if and only if E[log⁡η∣x]E[\log\eta\mid x]E[logη∣x] does not vary with xxx.

Lognormal: log⁡η∣x∼N(−s2(x)/2, s2(x))\log\eta\mid x\sim N\left(-s^2(x)/2,\ s^2(x)\right)logη∣x∼N(−s2(x)/2, s2(x)), so E[log⁡η∣x]=−s2(x)/2E[\log\eta\mid x]=-s^2(x)/2E[logη∣x]=−s2(x)/2. With s2(x)=0.2+γxs^2(x)=0.2+\gamma xs2(x)=0.2+γx and β=(0.5, 1)⊤\beta=(0.5,\,1)^\topβ=(0.5,1)⊤, E[log⁡y∣x]=0.4+(1−γ/2) xE[\log y\mid x]=0.4+(1-\gamma/2)\,xE[logy∣x]=0.4+(1−γ/2)x.

At γ=0.6\gamma=0.6γ=0.6 (x∼U(0,2)x\sim U(0,2)x∼U(0,2), N=20,000N=20{,}000N=20,000): log-OLS 0.6995 against its target 0.70; PPML 0.9807 against the true 1.

Zeros: log⁡0\log 0log0 is undefined, and dropping zeros or using log⁡(1+y)\log(1+y)log(1+y) changes the estimand; PPML keeps yi=0y_i=0yi​=0.

Many papers take logs of y and run OLS: a good estimator, of a different estimand. With a multiplicative error eta whose conditional mean is one, beta is the slope of the log of the mean. Taking logs first and averaging afterwards gives the boxed line, with an extra term: the conditional mean of log eta.

So log-OLS consistently estimates the slope of E of log y, which equals the slope we want if and only if E of log eta does not move with x, for example when eta has the same distribution shape at every x. The variance matters only through E of log eta.

In the lognormal case the mean of log eta is minus half its variance: the red band. Drag gamma. At zero the band has constant width and only the intercept is off. At 0.6, our simulation, the red line has slope 0.70 against the true 1; with 20,000 draws log-OLS gave 0.6995, right on its own target, and PPML 0.9807.

Zeros: the log of zero does not exist, and dropping zeros or adding one changes the estimand again. PPML keeps them.

直觉：先取对数再平均，和先平均再取对数，是两回事；只要 log η 的平均随 x 变，log-OLS 就在回答另一个问题，不是谁算错了。

True within-stratum ratios: 0.90/0.57=1.57890.90/0.57=1.57890.90/0.57=1.5789 (remote), 0.57/0.24=2.37500.57/0.24=2.37500.57/0.24=2.3750 (office). Observational: raw 2.8644 is 1.8891 times the imbalance fraction 1.5163 (q1=0.8333q_1=0.8333q1​=0.8333, q0=0.1667q_0=0.1667q0​=0.1667).

Back to the job offers. The score rows for the constant and salary make the fitted values add up to the observed acceptances in each salary group, the same move as in the AME proof. With a log link the fitted mean factorises. Divide the two group sums: the baseline cancels, leaving the salary factor times a ratio of average remote multipliers. Randomised, half of each group is remote, the fraction is one, and e to the beta is exactly 0.735 over 0.405, 1.8148, the risk ratio, without assuming that the exponential mean is correct.

Observational: the fraction is 1.5163, and the raw 2.8644 is 1.8891 times 1.5163, so PPML divides out the remote imbalance. But the truth has no single ratio, 1.5789 for remote and 2.3750 for office offers: 1.8891 is a design-weighted compromise.

The interval: 0.5960 with clustered SE 0.0551 is symmetric on the log scale, 0.4880 to 0.7040. Exponentiate and subtract one: plus 62.9 to plus 102.2 percent around 81.5, so 18.6 points below and 20.7 above. Report the two endpoints.

直觉：随机化让 PPML 的 exp(β) 恰好等于两组接受率之比；而区间在对数尺度上对称，换回百分比后因为指数函数是凸的，右边总比左边长。

Why OLS, logit and Poisson share one score equation

For OLS, logit and PPML the residual is orthogonal to every regressor, and only the shape of μi\mu_iμi​ changes.

GLS keeps the straight line but swaps the weight 1 for Ωg−1\nv{\Omega_g^{-1}}Ωg−1​, a block per respondent: ∑gXg⊤Ωg−1(yg−Xgβ)=0\textstyle\sum_g X_g^\top\nv{\Omega_g^{-1}}(y_g-X_g\beta)=0∑g​Xg⊤​Ωg−1​(yg​−Xg​β)=0 (Aitken 1935).

This is the derivation behind the one-equation slide. Logit and Poisson come from one family of densities, line one: the mean is the derivative of kappa, and the variance is a function of the mean, V of mu.

Line two: the score, by the chain rule. Line three: set it to zero; the scale drops out, and only the mean and the variance function survive. Line four: with the canonical link the derivative of the mean is V times x, so V cancels. The boxed line is the OLS normal equation with a different mean, for OLS, logit and PPML alike. GLS is the same equation with the matrix weight Omega inverse (Aitken 1935; textbook treatments in Greene 2018 and Verbeek 2017).

Click through the toggle in the order of the talk: the straight line for AMCE and OLS, the same line with block weights for GLS, the S-curve for logit, the exponential for PPML. The bottom line differs most: what you must believe for the equation to hold at the truth.

直觉：五个估计量都在让“残差和每个解释变量正交”；OLS、logit、PPML 的权重都是 1，GLS 则把同一个人的六次回答当成一组来加权。换的只是均值曲线的形状、权重，以及这个方程靠什么在总体里成立。

One sandwich gives every standard error

Each estimator solves ∑iψi(β^)=0\sum_i\psi_i(\hat\beta)=0∑i​ψi​(β^​)=0 (OLS: ψi=xi(yi−xi⊤β)\psi_i=x_i(y_i-x_i^\top\beta)ψi​=xi​(yi​−xi⊤​β); MLE: the score sis_isi​).

The bread belongs to the estimator. The meat is where sampling and grouping enter: every “which standard error?” debate is about BBB.

Divide by NNN (by GGG in the per-respondent rows) and replace expectations by sample averages to get the familiar estimates, e.g. s2(X⊤X)−1s^2(X^\top X)^{-1}s2(X⊤X)−1 and (X⊤Ω^−1X)−1(X^\top\hat\Omega^{-1}X)^{-1}(X⊤Ω^−1X)−1.

If all five solve one kind of equation, they share one distribution theory, derived once (Hayashi 2000; Wooldridge 2010). Expand the equation around the population root, beta star, and solve for the estimation error: the bracket converges to A by the law of large numbers, the scaled sum to a normal with variance B by the central limit theorem.

The bread A measures how sharply the equation responds to beta: it belongs to the estimator. The meat B measures how much the equation fluctuates from sample to sample: that is where sampling and grouping enter. Clustering only replaces row sums by respondent sums inside B (Liang and Zeger 1986; Cameron and Miller 2015).

Read the table from the bottom. For MLE and GLS the sandwich collapses to A inverse because B equals A, and only because we assumed something extra: a correct model, a correct Omega. Our logit's default SE, 0.1385, differs from the clustered 0.1336 for two reasons: the logit is misspecified, and one person's answers are correlated.

直觉：标准误永远是“面包夹肉”。面包来自估计量本身，肉来自数据怎么抽、怎么分组；“该报哪种标准误”的争论，其实都在争 B。

How much each estimator asks you to believe

For the number to mean what you wantExtra, for efficiencyWhat the standard error needs
AMCE Attributes randomised; no carryover across tasks; no profile-order effects (Hainmueller, Hopkins & Yamamoto 2014). Not a goal. Many independent respondents: cluster by respondent.
OLS E[xiεi]=0E[x_i\varepsilon_i]=0E[xi​εi​]=0. For a causal reading: salary as good as random given remote, and the same difference in every stratum. Constant variance, no correlation (A6, A7). Textbook: A5 to A7. HC1: independent rows. CR1: independent respondents.
GLS The OLS conditions, strengthened to strict exogeneity: E[cg+ugt∣Xg]=0E[c_g+u_{gt}\mid X_g]=0E[cg​+ugt​∣Xg​]=0 for all six rows of a respondent. The exchangeable Ω\OmegaΩ is the true covariance. Model-based: that Ω\OmegaΩ is right. Otherwise cluster.
Logit For a causal reading: salary as good as random given remote, and P(y=1∣x)=Λ(x⊤β)P(y=1\mid x)=\Lambda(x^\top\beta)P(y=1∣x)=Λ(x⊤β), the same odds ratio in every stratum. Otherwise a design-weighted compromise. Independent rows (with a correct mean, the Bernoulli distribution follows). Default: correct mean and independent rows (information equality). Otherwise cluster.
PPML For a causal reading: salary as good as random given remote, and E[y∣x]=exp⁡(x⊤β)E[y\mid x]=\exp(x^\top\beta)E[y∣x]=exp(x⊤β), the same ratio in every stratum; plus identification, finite moments, independent sampling. Var⁡(y∣x)∝μ\operatorname{Var}(y\mid x)\propto\muVar(y∣x)∝μ. Default: Var⁡(y∣x)=μ\operatorname{Var}(y\mid x)=\muVar(y∣x)=μ and independence. Otherwise cluster, with finite E[(y−μ)2xx⊤]E[(y-\mu)^2xx^\top]E[(y−μ)2xx⊤].

Consistency rests on the mean and the design behind it; efficiency on the variance; the standard error on how the data were sampled and grouped.

This is the table to photograph. Read it by columns. The first is question one, what number do I want, where all the arguments about the world happen. Only the AMCE row is free of a functional form: under randomisation the difference in means needs no model at all.

Outside randomisation every other row needs the same design condition as OLS, salary as good as random given remote, plus its own scale: the same difference, the same odds ratio or the same ratio in every stratum. Those are different beliefs, not stronger or weaker versions of one belief. GLS strengthens the OLS condition to strict exogeneity across all six of a person's answers.

The other two columns are extras: efficiency needs a variance model, and so does the default standard error; clustering by respondent removes that need. So the useful question is not which estimator is best, but which of these beliefs I can defend for this design.

直觉：一致性靠均值设定和背后的设计，效率靠方差设定，标准误靠抽样和分组。logit 和 PPML 并不比 OLS 少要设计，只是把“各层效应相同”换到了另一个尺度上。

Six things that sound right and are not

Sounds rightWhat is true
“The regression identifies the effect.” The design and its assumptions identify; the regression computes. In the observational design one command gives 0.5500 or 0.3300, depending on whether remote is controlled.
“Logit is the more correct model for a yes or no outcome.” No mean function is correct in advance. Logit assumes effects are constant in log-odds; here the truth is additive in probabilities, so logit misfits it: 0.88, 0.59, 0.59, 0.22 for 0.90, 0.57, 0.57, 0.24.
“Cluster-robust standard errors fix bias.” Clustering changes only the meat BBB. The estimate, and any bias in it, is untouched: 0.3300 under textbook, HC1 and CR1 alike.
“The observational SE rises because answers are clustered.” The rise from 0.0305 to 0.0369 is heteroskedasticity: once remote is controlled, salary's variation sits in the off-diagonal cells, where p(1−p)=0.245p(1-p)=0.245p(1−p)=0.245 is largest. Clustering adds only 0.0369 to 0.0385.
“Log-OLS is fine: heteroskedasticity only affects the SEs.” With y=exp⁡(x⊤β) ηy=\exp(x^\top\beta)\,\etay=exp(x⊤β)η, E[η∣x]=1E[\eta\mid x]=1E[η∣x]=1: log-OLS consistently estimates the slope of E[log⁡y∣x]E[\log y\mid x]E[logy∣x], but we want the slope of log⁡E[y∣x]\hl{\log E[y\mid x]}logE[y∣x]. They coincide if and only if E[log⁡η∣x]E[\log\eta\mid x]E[logη∣x] does not vary with xxx (simulation: log-OLS 0.6995, PPML 0.9807, truth 1.0).
“PPML needs count data.” It needs a correct mean E[y∣x]=exp⁡(x⊤β)E[y\mid x]=\exp(x^\top\beta)E[y∣x]=exp(x⊤β) with y≥0y\ge0y≥0, plus identification, moment and sampling conditions. It never assumed a Poisson distribution; our binary yyy gives a risk ratio, 1.8148.

Ask the room before each reveal: true or false? Every one of these sentences spends an assumption that serves one question on a different question.

One: identification comes from the design, not from the software. Two: logit is not more correct; it is a different functional-form belief, and here the wrong one. Three: clustering touches only the meat of the sandwich, never the estimate.

Four is the one people get wrong about our own example: the observational SE rises from 0.0305 to 0.0369 because salary's identifying variation lives in the noisiest cells, at 0.57. Clustering then adds only a little, to 0.0385.

Five: log-OLS is consistent, but for the slope of the expected log, not of the log of the expected value; they agree only when E of log eta does not change with x. Simulation: 0.6995 against PPML's 0.9807 and a true 1. Six: PPML is a set of moment conditions; it needs a correct mean, not integers (Santos Silva and Tenreyro 2006; Zou 2004 for binary outcomes).

直觉：这六句话的毛病都一样：把服务于一个问题的假设，拿去回答另一个问题。

Try it yourself

job_offer_example.py builds both designs and prints the estimates; it writes job_offer_example.csv (2,400 rows: design, respondent, high_salary, remote, accept). Python 3 and numpy only.

Python

import numpy as np
from job_offer_example import make_data, ols, glm

cells = {(1,1): 300, (1,0): 300, (0,1): 300, (0,0): 300}
resp, S, R, y = make_data(cells, seed=15)
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), S, R])
y = y.astype(float)

print(ols(X, y)[1])               # 0.33
b, mu, w = glm(X, y, 'logit')
print(np.exp(b[1]))               # odds ratio 5.0995
b, mu, w = glm(X, y, 'poisson')
print(np.exp(b[1]))               # ratio 1.8148

# observational: 500/100/100/500 rows, seed=1015

Stata

set seed 20261015
import delimited job_offer_example.csv, clear
keep if design=="randomised"

regress accept high_salary remote, ///
    vce(cluster respondent)     // 0.3300 (0.0240)

logit accept i.high_salary i.remote, ///
    vce(cluster respondent)     // 1.6291 (0.1336)
margins, dydx(high_salary)      // AME 0.3300

poisson accept high_salary remote, ///
    vce(cluster respondent) irr // 1.8148
                                // [1.6291, 2.0216]

The function glm is the one equation solved by Newton steps: it stops when X⊤(y−μ)=0X^\top(y-\mu)=0X⊤(y−μ)=0, for logit and Poisson alike.

Everything you have seen today can be rebuilt in a minute. The Python file needs only numpy, and its glm function is the one equation solved by Newton steps: it stops when X transpose times y minus mu is zero.

The Stata block reads the same CSV (comma-separated values) file; the seed line is only habit, nothing here is random. Use i.high_salary in the logit so that margins reports the discrete change, as our script does. The irr option gives the ratio with an asymmetric interval, 1.6291 to 2.0216; the lower end equals the logit coefficient by coincidence. Change the keep line to observational for the other column. One known difference: Stata's xtreg, re estimates the variance components differently, so its GLS coefficient is 0.3242 against our 0.3241.

直觉：所有数字都能在一分钟内复现；Python 里的 glm 函数就是那条方程本身，用牛顿法把 X'(y−μ) 推到零。
